son-cubano.name: Son Cubano
son-cubano.tagline: Foundational Cuban son, ancestor of salsa.
son-cubano.profile: Son cubano is a genre of music and dance originating in the highlands of eastern Cuba (Oriente - Sierra Maestra, Guantanamo, Baracoa, Santiago) in the late 19th century, a syncretic blend of Spanish (vocal style, guitar/tres, lyrical structure) and African Bantu (percussion, call-and-response) elements. Precursors include changui, nengon and kiriba. The classic 1920s Havana sextet standardized the format: tres, guitar, bongo, claves, maracas and double bass, later adding a trumpet (septeto). Danced by a couple, contratiempo (English Wikipedia; MasterClass).
son-cubano.insight: Son is widely called 'the father of salsa'; by the 1960s in New York it fused with other Latin styles to become salsa, and within Cuba it evolved into songo and timba (English Wikipedia).

bolero.name: Bolero
bolero.profile: The Cuban bolero is a slow, romantic vocal/song genre (also danced) that originated in Santiago de Cuba in the late 19th century - distinct from the older Spanish bolero in 3/4. 'Tristezas' by Jose 'Pepe' Sanchez (composed 1883) is regarded as the first bolero. It grew from the trova tradition of itinerant guitar-playing trovadores; in Cuba it is usually written in 2/4 with a son-related rhythm (bolero-son). It spread via the Trio Matamoros and Mexico's Trio Los Panchos across Latin America (English Wikipedia; UNESCO).
bolero.insight: The bolero was inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List in 2023 (file 01990) as a binational Cuba-Mexico element; UNESCO describes it as an indispensable part of the Latin American sentimental song (UNESCO).

mambo.name: Mambo
mambo.tagline: Cuban dance/music from the danzon-mambo, popularized by Perez Prado.
mambo.profile: Mambo is a Cuban dance and music genre. The music traces to the danzon de nuevo ritmo (danzon-mambo) created in the late 1930s by Orestes Lopez and Israel 'Cachao' Lopez in Antonio Arcano's charanga; the term derives from their 1938 danzon 'Mambo.' The original Cuban/Mexican ballroom dance (faster, less rigid than danzon) replaced rhumba as the fashionable US Latin dance; Damaso Perez Prado popularized it internationally from Mexico in the 1950s. A later New York breaking-step form became 'mambo on 2' (closely tied to salsa) (English Wikipedia).
mambo.insight: The original Cuban mambo dance had no basic breaking steps - Cuban dancers described it as 'feeling the music' - and US dance teachers standardized it for the commercial ballroom market (English Wikipedia).

cha-cha-cha.name: Cha Cha Cha
cha-cha-cha.tagline: Playful Cuban dance born from the danzon-mambo.
cha-cha-cha.profile: Cha-cha-cha is a Cuban dance and music genre introduced by composer/violinist Enrique Jorrin of the charanga Orquesta America in the early 1950s, developed from the danzon-mambo. Jorrin simplified the syncopation to make the music easier to dance; dancers at Havana's Silver Star Club improvised a triple step whose shuffling sound ('cha-cha-cha') named the genre. The first recordings, 'La enganadora' and 'Silver Star,' were recorded in March 1953 on Panart. The footwork resembles steps in Afro-Cuban Santeria dances. Played by charanga ensembles (English Wikipedia).
cha-cha-cha.insight: After the success of 'La enganadora,' cha-cha-cha eclipsed both mambo and danzon as the most popular dance style in Cuba, and by 1955 the craze had spread internationally; it became one of the five International Latin ballroom dances (English Wikipedia).

bachata.name: Bachata
bachata.era: 20th century; first single recorded 30 May 1962 (Jose Manuel Calderon)
bachata.tagline: Romantic Dominican guitar music and sensual partner dance.
bachata.profile: Bachata is a Dominican music-and-dance tradition that emerged in the 20th century from a fusion of rhythmic bolero with Afro-Antillean genres (Cuban son, cha-cha-cha, merengue). The dance is a couple's dance with sensual hip movement and a simple eight-step structure (side, side, tap/'pop'), in open or closed position. The typical group has five instruments: requinto (lead guitar), segunda (rhythm guitar), bass, bongos and guira. Lyrics express love and nostalgia; once stigmatized as 'musica de amargue' before globalizing via Juan Luis Guerra, Aventura and Romeo Santos (UNESCO; English Wikipedia).
bachata.insight: UNESCO inscribed 'Music and dance of Dominican Bachata' on the Representative List in 2019 (file 01514, decision 14.COM 10.b.10); whereas the merengue bid took 12 years, the bachata bid was expedited in two (Listin Diario via DR1.com, 2019; UNESCO).

Its rural forms (notably samba de roda, Bahia) fed the urban 'samba carioca' of early-20th-century Rio de Janeiro, which became central to Carnival and a symbol of Brazilian national identity. tango.name: Tango
tango.tagline: Iconic Río de la Plata partner dance and global musical genre.
tango.profile: Tango is a partner and social dance and musical genre that originated in the 1880s in the impoverished port neighborhoods along the Río de la Plata (Buenos Aires and Montevideo), born from Argentine milonga, Spanish-Cuban habanera, and Uruguayan candombe. It encompasses a family of related dances (tango, vals, milonga) and styles ranging from close-embrace milonguero to open salon and stage tango (English Wikipedia). The bandoneón is its signature instrument.
tango.insight: Tango is the most recognizable embodiment of Río de la Plata identity and the only fully UNESCO-inscribed dance in this region's catalog (2009); it both embodies and encourages diversity and cultural dialogue (UNESCO; English Wikipedia).

candombe.tagline: Afro-Argentine drum-and-dance heritage of Buenos Aires barrios.
candombe.profile: Candombe is an Afro-Río de la Plata music-and-dance tradition. The Argentine (porteño) form, centered in Buenos Aires neighborhoods such as Monserrat, San Telmo, and La Boca, is played on two main hand drums - the 'llamador' (bass) and 'repicador' (sharp) - and danced by comparsas in street parades (llamadas) (English Wikipedia). The Argentine variety became largely private due to demographic decline and carnival bans, but is reviving in public street parades.
candombe.insight: Argentine candombe is a key root of milonga and tango and a living marker of Afro-Argentine identity; the Kikongo-derived word and the 'tangós' gathering places gave rise to the term tango (English Wikipedia; Buenos Aires City Government).

breaking.name: Breaking
breaking.tagline: The Bronx, 1970s — when b-boys turned cardboard into a stage and gravity into a suggestion.
breaking.profile: Breakdancing or breaking, also called b-boying (when performed by men) or b-girling (women), is a style of street dance developed by African Americans and Puerto Ricans in the Bronx borough of New York City. Breakdancing consists mainly of four kinds of movement—toprock, footwork, power moves, and freezes—and is typically set to songs containing drum breaks, especially in funk, soul, and hip-hop. Its modern dance elements originated among the poor youth of New York during the 1970s and early 1980s. It is tied to the birth of hip-hop, whose DJs played songs featuring rhythmic breaks for dancers.
breaking.insight: Breaking would become so popular, it was featured at performances like the 1984 LA Olympics, providing people worldwide with their first experience of breaking. In 1991 the first international breaking competition, Battle of the Year, was held in Hanover Germany.

bharatanatyam.name: Bharatanatyam
bharatanatyam.tagline: Tamil Nadu's temple-born classical dance of mudras and aramandi
bharatanatyam.profile: Bharatanatyam is a major Indian classical dance form originating in Tamil Nadu, recognized by the Sangeet Natak Akademi as one of India's oldest classical dance forms (Wikipedia). It is noted for a fixed upper torso, bent legs and flexed knees (aramandi), intricate footwork, and a vocabulary of hand, eye and facial gestures, accompanied by Carnatic music and a nattuvanar conductor (Wikipedia). Its repertoire spans nritta (pure dance), nritya (expression) and natya (drama). Once a temple dance known as Sadir/Sadiraattam, it was renamed Bharatanatyam around 1932 and revived for the public stage in the 20th century (ipassio).

hora.profile: Hora, also known as horo and oro, is a type of circle dance traditionally performed in Southeast Europe. locking.name: Locking
locking.tagline: Los Angeles, 1969 — Don Campbell froze mid-move, and the freeze became a vocabulary.
locking.profile: Locking is a style of funk dance. The name is based on the concept of locking movements, which means freezing from a fast movement and "locking" in a certain position, holding that position for a short while and then continuing at the same speed as before. The movements are generally large and exaggerated, and often very rhythmic and tightly synced with the music.
locking.insight: Locking was invented in 1969 by Don 'Campbellock' Campbell in Los Angeles, who originated the freeze-and-point move on Soul Train; the Lockers (Toni Basil, Fred Berry) made it a national phenomenon by 1973.

tap-dance.name: Tap Dance
tap-dance.tagline: African American vaudeville — feet that became their own percussion section.
tap-dance.profile: Tap dance (or tap) is a form of dance that uses the sounds of tap shoes striking the floor as a form of percussion; it is often accompanied by music. Tap dancing can also be performed with no musical accompaniment; the sound of the taps is its own music. It is an American art form that evolved alongside the advent of jazz music. Tap is a type of step dance that began with the combination of Black American and Irish dance traditions, such as the juba dance and Irish step dances.

foxtrot.profile: The foxtrot is a smooth, progressive dance characterized by long, continuous flowing movements across the dance floor. It is danced to big band (usually vocal) music. The dance is similar in its look to waltz, although the rhythm is in a 44 time signature instead of 34. Developed in the 1910s, the foxtrot reached its height of popularity in the 1930s and remains practiced today.

paso-doble.name: Paso Doble
paso-doble.tagline: Spain — the bullfight rendered as dance. He is the matador, she is the cape.
paso-doble.profile: Pasodoble is the Spanish bullfight dance — the lead steps as the matador, the follower flowing like the muleta cape, the rhythm a driving 2/4 march. Originated in late-18th-century Spanish military marches and codified into a competitive ballroom form in the early 20th century, pasodoble is the most theatrical of the five International Latin dances. The most iconic pasodoble tune — 'España Cañí' — opens every Spanish bullfight to this day.
paso-doble.insight: It was composed in 1957, with lyrics by Guillermo González Ospina and music by Juan Mari Asins inspired by the Spanish classic "España cañí". These dances, developed around 1538, were a gradual combination of Castillian music and dance with the "garrotín", a fast and repetitive Romani couples dance, adapted into a march form.

jive.name: Jive
jive.tagline: 1940s American GIs — what the rest of the world danced when American swing crossed the Atlantic.
jive.profile: The jive is a dance style that originated in the United States from African Americans in the early 1930s. The name of the dance comes from the name of a form of African-American vernacular slang, popularized in the 1930s by the publication of a dictionary by Cab Calloway, the famous jazz bandleader and singer. In competition ballroom dancing, the jive is often (mistakenly) grouped with the Latin-inspired ballroom dances, though its roots are based more on swing dancing than Latin dancing.
jive.insight: Jive was officially banned in the Soviet Union until the 1980s — caught dancers risked deportation to labor camps.

bhangra.name: Bhangra
bhangra.tagline: Energetic Punjabi harvest folk dance driven by the dhol
bhangra.profile: Bhangra is a vigorous folk dance of the Punjab region of the Indian subcontinent, especially associated with the spring Vaisakhi harvest festival (Wikipedia). Dancers perform energetic kicks, leaps and shoulder movements to short sung couplets (boliyan) and the syncopated beat of the double-headed dhol drum (Britannica). Its purest traditional form is traced to the Sialkot area; modern staged bhangra developed in the 1950s, notably patronized by the Maharaja of Patiala who requested a performance in 1953 (Wikipedia). The Punjabi diaspora spread bhangra worldwide, fusing it with hip-hop, house and reggae.
bhangra.insight: Originally a men's dance, bhangra drew its name from bhang (hemp), a Vaisakhi harvest product, and second-generation diaspora Punjabi women later embraced it, sometimes at the expense of the traditional women's giddha (Britannica).

hula.name: Hula
hula.era: Ancient/pre-contact origins; revived under King Kalakaua (1874-1891)
hula.tagline: Sacred Hawaiian dance of chant, gesture and storytelling
hula.profile: Hula is the traditional dance of Native Hawaiians, integrating chanted poetry (mele/oli), rhythmic movement and a vocabulary of hand gestures that depict nature, emotions and narrative (Wikipedia). Many hula are religious performances dedicated to deities; dancers learning sacred hula were ritually secluded under the protection of Laka, goddess of hula, in a halau (Wikipedia). American Protestant missionaries arriving in 1820 denounced and nearly suppressed hula; King David Kalakaua revived it in the late 19th century (New World Encyclopedia). Forms range from ancient hula kahiko to modern hula auana.
hula.insight: Hawaiian tradition links hula's origin to several gods and humans - including Laka and Pele's sister Hiiaka - and the Pukui-Elbert dictionary notes the word 'hula' was not in general use until after the mid-1800s (Kaimi Institute).

tarantella.tagline: Southern Italy — once thought to cure the spider bite by sweating out the venom in dance.
tarantella.profile: Tarantella (Italian: [taranˈtɛlla]) is a group of various southern Italian folk dances originating in the regions of Calabria, Campania, Sicilia, and Apulia. It is characterized by a fast upbeat tempo, usually in 68 time (sometimes 128 or 44), accompanied by tambourines. It is among the most recognized forms of traditional southern Italian music. The specific dance-name varies with every region, for instance sonu a ballu in Calabria, tammurriata in Campania, and pizzica in Salento. Tarantella is popular in southern Italy, Greece, and Malta.

zouk.name: Zouk
zouk.tagline: Guadeloupe and Martinique, 1979 — Kassav' invented zouk by speeding up Caribbean rhythms with synthesizers.
zouk.profile: Zouk is a musical movement and dance pioneered by the French Antillean band Kassav' in the early 1980s. It was originally characterized by a fast tempo (120–145 bpm), a percussion-driven rhythm, and a loud horn section. Musicians from Martinique and Guadeloupe eventually added MIDI instrumentation to their compas style, which developed into a genre called zouk-love. Zouk-love is effectively the French Lesser Antilles' compas, and it gradually became indistinguishable from compas.
zouk.insight: It was originally characterized by a fast tempo (120–145 bpm), a percussion-driven rhythm, and a loud horn section.

reggaeton.profile: Reggaeton (UK: , US: ) is a style of popular and electronic music that originated in Panama during the late 1980s. It has been popularized and dominated by artists from Puerto Rico since the early 1990s. It has evolved from dancehall, with elements of hip hop, Latin American, and Caribbean music. Vocals include toasting/rapping and singing or rap-singing, typically in Spanish. Reggaeton is regarded as one of the most popular music genres in the Spanish-speaking Caribbean.
reggaeton.insight: Four reggaeton songs were sung at the 2005 MTV Video Music Awards: by Don Omar , Tego Calderón, Daddy Yankee, and Shakira with Sanz – the first time any reggaeton song was performed on that stage. The success of the song and its remix version led Daddy Yankee to become the most listened-to artist worldwide on the streaming service Spotify on 9 July 2017, being the first Latin artist to do so.

marinera.name: Marinera
marinera.tagline: Peru — handkerchief courtship dance renamed in 1879 to honor the Navy after Chile invaded during the War of the Pacific.
marinera.profile: Marinera is a partner dance that originated along the coastal regions of Peru, using handkerchiefs as props. The dance is a re-enactment of an ancient Mochic dance, modernised with a mix of Spanish contradanza and Andean zamacueca, and is a stylized reenactment of a courtship, showing a blend of the different cultures of Peru. The dance has gained recognition throughout South America and is known as the most prominent traditional dance of Peru. The city of Trujillo has been recognized as the national birthplace of the marinera since 1986.
marinera.insight: The first Marinera to be written in musical notation was La Concheperla composed by Abelardo Gamarra Rondó and José Alvarado, by Rosa Mercedes Ayarza de Morales in 1894... The city of Trujillo has been recognized as the national birthplace of the marinera since 1986.

hopak.name: Hopak
hopak.tagline: Ukraine's Cossack national dance — split-leaps, spinning kicks, athletic combat-training as performance.
hopak.profile: Hopak (Ukrainian: гопак, IPA: [ɦoˈpɑk]) is a Ukrainian folk dance originating as a male dance among the Zaporozhian Cossacks, but later danced by couples, male soloists, and mixed groups of dancers. It is performed most often as a solitary concert dance by amateur and professional Ukrainian dance ensembles, as well as other performers of folk dances. It has also been incorporated into larger artistic opuses such as operas, ballets and theatre. The hopak is often popularly referred to as the "National Dance of Ukraine" and has become very popular in Poland.
hopak.insight: In the spring of 1935, the All-Union Organization of Cultural Relations with Foreign Countries agreed to send a delegation to the upcoming First International Festival of the Folk Dance in London.

khon.profile: Khon (Thai: โขน, pronounced [kʰǒːn]) is a dance drama genre from Thailand. Khon has been performed since the Ayutthaya Kingdom. Born from the harmonious blend of traditional Thai performing arts, Khon has flourished into a distinctive cultural treasure of Thailand. It is traditionally performed solely in the royal court by men in masks accompanied by narrators and a traditional piphat ensemble. A variation of this genre with female performers is called khon phu ying (โขนผู้หญิง).

haka.name: Haka
haka.tagline: Aotearoa New Zealand — Māori chant and challenge. The ground itself answers.
haka.profile: Haka (; singular and plural haka, in both Māori and New Zealand English) are a variety of ceremonial dances in Māori culture. A performance art, haka are often performed by a group, with vigorous movements and stamping of the feet with rhythmically shouted accompaniment. Haka have been traditionally performed by both men and women for a variety of social functions within Māori culture. They are performed to welcome distinguished guests, or to acknowledge great achievements, occasions, or funerals. Kapa haka groups are common in schools.
haka.insight: Prince Alfred, the Duke of Edinburgh, was the first royal to visit New Zealand, in 1869. In September 2024, thousands gathered in Eden Park in Auckland to break the record of the largest haka performance.

dabke.name: Dabke
dabke.tagline: Levantine stomping line dance led by a handkerchief-waving lawweeh
dabke.profile: Dabke is the Levantine folk line dance performed at weddings and celebrations across Lebanon, Syria, Jordan, Palestine and Iraq (Wikipedia). Dancers link hands in a line or semicircle and stamp and jump in synchronised six-beat patterns; the line is led by a lawweeh (raas) who waves a handkerchief or string of beads (masbaha), improvising leaps and breaks (Wikipedia; iHeritage). The name derives from Levantine Arabic dabaka, 'stamping of the feet'; folklore links its stomping origin to communally tamping mud rooftops (Bayt Al Fann).
dabke.insight: Though a powerful emblem of Lebanese identity, dabke is shared across the whole Levant and is not uniquely Lebanese. After the launch of the Baalbek International Festival in 1956, Soviet dance expert Igor Moiseyev was invited to assess Lebanese folk traditions and proposed a standardized choreography (The Beiruter; iHeritage).

sufi-whirling.name: Sufi Whirling
sufi-whirling.tagline: Konya, Turkey, 1273 — 60 rotations per minute, maintained for hours. Right palm to heaven, left palm to earth.
sufi-whirling.profile: Sufi whirling (or Sufi turning) (Turkish: Semazen borrowed from Persian Sama-zan, Sama, meaning listening, from Arabic, and zan, meaning doer, from Persian) is a form of physically active meditation which originated among certain Sufi groups, and which is still practiced by the Sufi dervishes of the Mevlevi order and other orders such as the Rifa'i-Marufi. It is a customary meditation practice performed within the sema, or worship ceremony, through which dervishes (from the Persian darvish درویش, also called semazens, from Persian سماعزن) aim to reach greater connection with Allah.
sufi-whirling.insight: In 1925, Turkey ordered the dissolution of all Sufi fraternities by decree, the Mevlevi managed to survive among small villages throughout the Middle East. In 1954, the Turkish government granted the Mevlevi order a special permission to perform ritual whirling practices for tourists during two weeks each year.

It originated in Hungary and was popularized by bands in Hungary as well as neighboring countries and regions such as of Slovenia, Burgenland, Croatia, Transylvania, Slovakia, Vojvodina and Moravia, as well as among the Banat Bulgarians, including those in Bulgaria. The original folk csárdás, as opposed to the later international variants, is enjoying a revival in Hungary thanks to the táncház movement.

mazurka.name: Mazurka
mazurka.tagline: Polish countryside — Chopin made the rural triple meter into European concert music.
mazurka.profile: The Mazurka (Polish: mazurek, GEN. mazurka) is a Polish musical form based on stylised folk dances in triple metre, usually at a lively tempo, with character defined mostly by the prominent mazur's "strong accents unsystematically placed on the second or third beat". The Mazurka, alongside the polka dance, became popular at the ballrooms and salons of Europe in the 19th century, particularly through the notable works by Frédéric Chopin.
mazurka.insight: In 1825, Maria Szymanowska wrote the largest collection of piano mazurkas published before Chopin. Henryk Wieniawski also wrote two for violin with piano , Julian Cochran composed a collection of five mazurkas for solo piano and orchestra, and in the 1920s, Karol Szymanowski wrote a set of twenty for piano and finished his composing career with a final pair in 1934.

sirtaki.name: Sirtaki
sirtaki.tagline: The 1964 'Zorba's Dance' - Greece's famous invented dance.
sirtaki.profile: A 20th-century choreographed dance created for the 1964 film 'Zorba the Greek.' Mikis Theodorakis's 'Zorba's Dance' adapted a traditional Chania syrtos tune by composer Giorgis Koutsourelis; the film choreography is attributed to Giorgos Provias. It is NOT a traditional folk dance but an amalgam of slow hasapiko and faster hasaposerviko, with syrtos (dragging) and pidikhtos (hopping) elements. Danced in line or circle, hands on neighbours' shoulders; meter 4/4 accelerating, often shifting to 2/4 in the fast part, beginning slow then becoming vigorous with hops and leaps. Bouzouki-led music; performed at tavernas, weddings and festivals (English Wikipedia; Society of Folk Dance Historians).
sirtaki.insight: Despite global fame as 'Greek,' sirtaki is an invented tradition created for cinema; Anthony Quinn had a broken foot during filming, and the dragging-sliding steps replaced the planned hopping steps because he could not perform the dances taught to him (English Wikipedia).

tinikling.name: Tinikling
tinikling.tagline: The Philippines' national dance — dancers leap between bamboo poles clapping at lightning speed.
tinikling.profile: Tinikling (traditionally written tiniclín) is a traditional Philippine folk dance which originated prior to Spanish colonialism in the area. The dance involves at least two people beating, tapping, and sliding bamboo poles on the ground and against each other in coordination with one or more dancers who step over and in between the poles in a dance. It is traditionally danced to rondalla music, a sort of serenade played by an ensemble of stringed instruments which originated in Spain during the Middle Ages. The locomotor movements used in this dance are hopping, jumping, and turning.
tinikling.insight: Tinikling takes its name from the tikling bird — the slender Gallirallus philippensis whose graceful leg movements through rice paddies inspired the choreography; the dance literally translates as 'doing it like the tikling.' Today the Bayanihan Philippine National Folk Dance Company carries Tinikling to global stages, and Filipino schools teach the basics from primary level — a Filipino who can't dance Tinikling is rare anywhere in the world.

odissi.name: Odissi
odissi.era: Ancient roots (2nd-c BCE evidence); revived mid-20th c
odissi.tagline: Odisha's lyrical temple classical dance of tribhanga and chowk
odissi.profile: Odissi (formerly Orissi) is an ancient Indian classical dance that originated in the temples of Odisha, performed predominantly by women to express religious stories, especially of Vaishnavism (Wikipedia). Its technique is built around the chowk (a square, masculine stance) and the tribhanga (a feminine three-bend posture), with fluid movements and emphasis on bhakti bhava (devotion) (Britannica). Theoretical roots trace to the Natya Shastra's Odra-Magadhi style, with dance poses evidenced in the Udayagiri-Khandagiri caves and temple sculptures at Konark and Puri (Wikipedia).
odissi.insight: Historically sustained by Mahari temple dancers and Gotipua boy dancers, Odissi was reconstructed and won Sangeet Natak Akademi recognition in the late 1950s through gurus such as Kelucharan Mohapatra and Pankaj Charan Das (Sahapedia).

kathakali.name: Kathakali
kathakali.tagline: Kerala's grand masked dance-drama of gods and demons
kathakali.profile: Kathakali ('story-play') is a classical dance-drama of Kerala and one of the most complex forms of Indian theatre, native to the Malayalam-speaking region (Wikipedia). It enacts verses (Attakatha) drawn from the Ramayana, Mahabharata and Puranas, using the navarasa facial expressions of the Natya Shastra, an elaborate hand-gesture system, vivid stylized makeup and large costumes (Kerala Tourism). It evolved in the 17th century from earlier traditions such as Kutiyattam and Krishnanattam and incorporates footwork from the Kalaripayattu martial art; performances are accompanied by Chenda and Maddalam drums and sopanam-style singing (Wikipedia).
kathakali.insight: Kathakali's gesture language is built on 24 basic mudras which, with combinations, yield a total of 470 symbols per the Hasthalakshana Deepika gesture manual (cyberkerala.com); the art was refined and institutionalized at the Kerala Kalamandalam, founded by poet Vallathol Narayana Menon in 1930.

gumboot.name: Gumboot
gumboot.tagline: South African gold mines — workers communicated by stomping gumboots and slapping chains when speech was forbidden in the mineshafts.
gumboot.profile: The gumboot dance (or Isicathulo) is a South African dance that is performed by dancers wearing Wellington boots. In South Africa these are more commonly called gumboots. The boots may be embellished with bells, so that they ring as the dancers stamp on the ground. This sound would be a code or a different calling to say something to another person a short distance away. This was used to communicate in the mines as there was strictly no talking otherwise there would be severe, drastic punishments at the discretion of their superior.
gumboot.insight: It was commissioned by Carnegie Hall in 2008 and can be heard in full on their website, performed by Todd Palmer and the St. In 2017, World of Step was established by Creative Director, Chuck Maldonado and Founder of Art of Stepping, Jessica 'Remo' Saul in direct response of preserve the historical component of gumboot dance to be shared to the mass.

joropo.name: Joropo
joropo.tagline: Venezuelan and Colombian plains — harp, cuatro, maracas, and a heel-toe stomp built for hard ground.
joropo.profile: The joropo, better known as Música Llanera, is a musical style resembling the fandango, and an accompanying dance. It originated in the Llanos of Colombia and Venezuela 300 years ago and it has African, European and Native South American influences. There are different joropo variants: tuyero, oriental, and llanero. It is a fundamental genre of Venezuelan música criolla. It is also the most popular "folk rhythm": the well-known song "Alma Llanera" is a joropo, considered the unofficial national anthem of Venezuela. In 1882 it became Venezuela's national dance and music.
joropo.insight: In 2025, UNESCO inscribed Venezuelan joropo on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. The Colombian Congress declared joropo as “Cultural Heritage of the Nation” in 2025 and designated May 24 as National Joropo Day.

bomba.name: Bomba

bomba.profile: Bomba is an umbrella term that refers to a variety of musical styles and associated dances originating in Puerto Rico. It was developed during the 17th century by enslaved Africans and their descendants on sugar plantations along coastal towns, most notably Loiza, Mayagüez, Ponce, and San Juan. It is the island's oldest musical tradition. Bomba reflects a syncretism of Puerto Rico’s many cultural groups.
bomba.insight: The first documentation of bomba dates to 1797, when botanist André Pierre Ledru described his impressions of inhabitants dancing and singing popular bombas in Voyage aux îles de Ténériffe, la Trinité, Saint-Thomas, Sainte-Croix et Porto Ricco. In 1998, Son del Batey was founded in San Juan, Puerto Rico, by a group of college students at the University of Puerto Rico in Mayagüez.

chacarera.tagline: Lively Santiago del Estero couple dance with stomping and clapping.
chacarera.profile: The chacarera is a fast, festive couples folk dance from Santiago del Estero, the rural counterpart to cosmopolitan tango. Dancers face each other without touching; men circle the women with foot-stomping (zapateo) and finger-snapping (castañetas) while women perform the swirling zarandeo, ending with the 'coronación' embrace. It is accompanied by guitar, violin, bombo legüero, and voice, sung in coplas; chacarera simple and doble are the main variants (English Wikipedia; Carnegie Hall).
chacarera.insight: Standardized by Andrés Chazarreta's early-20th-century scores and the 1950s recordings of Los Hermanos Ábalos, the chacarera became a nationwide emblem of Argentine nativism and rural identity (English Wikipedia).

zamba.name: Zamba
zamba.era: 19th century (derived from Peruvian zamacueca via Chilean cueca)
zamba.tagline: Elegant northwestern courtship dance of waving white handkerchiefs.
zamba.profile: Zamba is a slow, elegant couples folk dance and music genre of northwestern Argentina (Salta, Tucumán). In 6/8, couples circle each other without touching, waving white handkerchiefs (pañuelos) to enact a poetic courtship of invitation, acceptance, and gentle rejection; women also work their wide skirts. It is played on guitar and bombo legüero, sometimes with violin (English Wikipedia; Dale Folklore). It derives from the Peruvian zamacueca and shares elements with the cueca.
zamba.insight: Often called the 'queen' of Argentine folk dances and once considered the national dance, zamba is a centerpiece of festivals like Cosquín; its name comes from the colonial term 'zambo' (mixed ancestry), distinct from Brazilian samba (English Wikipedia).

lambada.name: Lambada
lambada.tagline: Para-origin couples dance, a 1989 global sensation.
lambada.profile: Lambada is a partner dance (and music genre) originating in Para, northern Brazil, fusing carimbo with Caribbean and other rhythms. Danced in close embrace with pronounced hip movement and arched turns, often with short skirts and circular motion, it became a worldwide craze in 1989 via Kaoma's single 'Lambada' (English Wikipedia).
lambada.insight: Kaoma's 'Lambada' (1989) sold millions worldwide and topped charts in over 15 countries; per English Wikipedia it was the most successful European single in the history of CBS Records. Lambada is the direct parent of Brazilian Zouk.

maracatu.name: Maracatu
maracatu.tagline: Pernambuco Afro-Brazilian procession; nacao and rural forms.
maracatu.profile: Maracatu denotes several performance genres of Pernambuco. Maracatu nacao (de baque virado, 'turned-around beat') is an Afro-Brazilian processional genre of Recife/Olinda rooted in the coronations of the Reis do Congo, featuring a royal court (king, queen, dama do paco carrying the calunga doll), a percussion group of 80-100 (alfaias, gongue, tarol, ganzas) and Candomble/Jurema ties. Maracatu rural (de baque solto), from the sugarcane Zona da Mata, is Afro-Indigenous, centered on the caboclo de lanca (English Wikipedia; IPHAN).
maracatu.insight: IPHAN registered Maracatu Nacao as Patrimonio Cultural do Brasil in 2014; the oldest continuously active rural group dates to the late 19th/early 20th century (English Wikipedia; IPHAN).

bambuco.profile: A couples courtship dance-song of the Colombian Andes (Huila, Tolima, Cundinamarca), in 6/8-3/4 sesquialtera, performed by string ensembles of tiple, bandola and guitar (Britannica; Colombia Country Brand). cueca.name: Cueca
cueca.era: Late 18th century to present; form consolidated by late 19th century
cueca.profile: A couples courtship dance in which partners wave handkerchiefs and trace circular figures, turns and half-turns, evoking the courtship of a rooster and hen (Britannica; Wikipedia). Danced to guitar, accordion, guitarron, harp, tambourine and handclaps, in alternating 6/8-3/4 with hemiola; structured in cuarteta, seguidilla and remate. Central to the September Fiestas Patrias; widely held to descend from the Peruvian zamacueca. Declared Chile's national dance by Decree No. 23 (Diario Oficial, 6 November 1979) (Marca Chile; Wikipedia).
cueca.insight: The Pinochet dictatorship's official promotion of cueca from 1979 reshaped its imagery; in protest the cueca sola debuted on 8 March 1978 in Santiago by the folk ensemble of the Association of Families of the Detained-Disappeared (AFDD), per Chile's Museo de la Memoria y los Derechos Humanos.

two-step.name: Two-step
two-step.tagline: Texas dance halls — the everyman's country-western partner dance. Two quick, two slow, forever.
two-step.profile: The two-step is a step found in various dances, including many folk dances. A two-step consists of two steps in approximately the same direction onto the same foot, separated by a joining or uniting step with the other foot. For example, a right two-step forward is a forward step onto the right foot, a closing step with the left foot, and a forward step onto the right foot. The closing step may be done directly beside the other foot, or obliquely beside, or even crossed, as long as the closing foot does not go past the other foot.
two-step.insight: The original Two-step was a simple dance that first caught on with the public when John Philip Sousa came out with the 'Washington Post March' in 1889." == Europe == In Europe the two-step became popular from around 1900 until the 1910s, when the one-step and the foxtrot took over.

west-coast-swing.name: West Coast Swing

west-coast-swing.profile: West Coast Swing is a partner dance with roots in Lindy Hop, characterized by an elastic look that results from its extension-compression technique of partner connection. It is danced primarily in a slotted area on the dance floor. The dance allows for both partners to improvise steps while dancing together, putting West Coast Swing in a short list of dances that emphasize improvisation. Typically the follower is led forward into new patterns traveling forward on counts "1" and "2" of each basic pattern, rather than rocking back.
west-coast-swing.insight: There is never only one way to do anything." In 1994 Blair noted that the posture for men had trended to be more upright than in previous years. Western swing, country boogie, and, with a smaller audience, jump blues were popular on the West Coast throughout the 1940s and into the 1950s when they were renamed and marketed as rock and roll in 1954.

khorovod.profile: The khorovod or horovod (Russian: хоровод, Ukrainian: хоровод, корогод, Polish: korowód) is the Slavic name for a folk dance combining circle dance and chorus singing, similar to the choreia of ancient Greece.
khorovod.insight: Khorovod survived a thousand years of cultural pressure: the Orthodox Church suppressed it for centuries as 'pagan ritual,' Peter the Great's Westernizing reforms marginalized it in favor of European court dance, and Soviet anti-religion campaigns banned its ceremonial use. highland-fling.name: Highland Fling
highland-fling.tagline: The Highlands of Scotland — danced on a warrior's shield. The tight footwork is because the shield was that small.
highland-fling.profile: The Highlands of Scotland — competitive solo dance traditionally performed on the shield of a fallen enemy. The tight footwork developed because the shield was that small. Performed at every Royal Edinburgh Military Tattoo since 1950; competitive Highland dance is a Commonwealth Games invitational sport.
highland-fling.insight: The Scottish Highland Fling was traditionally danced atop a small round shield called a targe — points of the targe's central spike were intended to discipline the dancer's footwork; the modern competitive Fling has been governed by the Scottish Official Board of Highland Dancing since 1950.

hambo.tagline: Sweden — the country's most-danced partner dance. Every Midsummer ends with a hambo around the maypole.
hambo.profile: Sweden — the country's most-danced partner dance. Every Midsummer in Sweden ends with at least one hambo around the maypole. A triple-meter turning dance descended from older Scandinavian polskor; flowing, danced in closed embrace, with a small step on every beat.
hambo.insight: Hambo became Sweden's national dance after Hjalmar Mörk's 1898 manual standardized its 3/4 rhythm and turning-couple form; Skansen open-air museum has hosted public hambo every Friday evening throughout summer since 1891.

pavane.name: Pavane
pavane.tagline: Renaissance Europe — the slow processional dance once used at funerals. Dancers wore swords because nobody could move fast enough to fight.
pavane.profile: Renaissance Europe, 1500s — the slow processional dance once used at funerals in Spain and Italy. Dancers wore swords because nobody could move quickly enough to fight. Maurice Ravel's 1899 "Pavane pour une infante défunte" preserved its melody for the modern world.
pavane.insight: Italian dancing master Fabritio Caroso codified the pavane in his 1581 manual 'Il Ballarino'; the dance's stately tempo of 60-70 beats per minute matched the resting heartbeat of European nobility — making it the slowest formal dance in 16th-century court culture.

manipuri.name: Manipuri
manipuri.era: Roots in ritual traditions; raslila formalized 18th century
manipuri.tagline: Manipur's gentle devotional classical dance of Krishna's raslila
manipuri.profile: Manipuri dance is a major Indian classical dance form from the northeastern state of Manipur, distinguished by gentle, fluid, gliding movements in which the feet rarely strike the floor hard (Wikipedia). A confluence of ritual traditions - Lai Haraoba, Huyen Langlon, Nata Sankirtana and Raslila - its best-known expression is the Raas Leela depicting the love of Krishna, Radha and the gopis, alongside the vigorous male Pung Cholom drum dance (Wikipedia). The dance is devotional in nature, rooted in Vaishnavism with themes also from Shaktism and Shaivism.
manipuri.insight: Under King Bhagyachandra (Ching Thang Khomba) in the 18th century the raslila was formalized, and Manipuri gained wider recognition after poet Rabindranath Tagore witnessed a performance in 1917 and introduced its teaching at Visva-Bharati, Santiniketan (Britannica).

mohiniyattam.name: Mohiniyattam
mohiniyattam.era: Term first attested 16th century; systematized 18th-19th c; revived 1930
mohiniyattam.tagline: Kerala's graceful solo lasya 'dance of the enchantress'
mohiniyattam.profile: Mohiniyattam is an Indian classical dance from Kerala, named after Mohini, the female enchantress avatar of Vishnu (Wikipedia). Following the gentle, feminine lasya style of the Natya Shastra, it is traditionally a solo dance by women, with delicate swaying movements, subtle facial expression, Carnatic-style music and lyrics in the Sanskrit-Malayalam hybrid Manipravalam (Wikipedia). The term is first attested in the 16th-century Vyavaharamala; the dance was systematized under Travancore king Swathi Thirunal but later ridiculed and banned (1931-38) during the colonial anti-nautch movement before being revived (Wikipedia).
mohiniyattam.insight: Mohiniyattam was revived and reconstructed largely through poet Vallathol Narayana Menon, who founded the Kerala Kalamandalam in 1930 to restore Kerala's classical arts (Britannica).

bon-odori.name: Bon Odori
bon-odori.tagline: Buddhist summer ancestor-honoring folk dance, parent of regional Bon dances
bon-odori.profile: Bon Odori ('Bon dance') is the umbrella style of folk dancing performed during the Buddhist Obon festival to welcome and honour the spirits of ancestors, with a history of nearly 600 years originating in the Nenbutsu odori (Wikipedia, Obon). A typical Bon dance has people circling a raised wooden scaffold (yagura) in yukata, accompanied by regional min'yo folk songs - so the dance looks and sounds different region to region (e.g. Soran Bushi in Hokkaido, Gujo Odori in Gifu, Awa Odori in Tokushima) (Nippon.com).
bon-odori.insight: Per Wikipedia, Bon Odori originates from the story of Maha Maudgalyayana (Mokuren), a disciple of the Buddha who danced with joy upon freeing his mother's spirit - making it fundamentally a dance of gratitude to ancestors.

lion-dance.name: Lion Dance
lion-dance.era: Tang dynasty or earlier (by 3rd c. CE)
lion-dance.tagline: Two dancers animate an auspicious lion to martial drumming
lion-dance.profile: The lion dance (舞獅, wǔshī) is a traditional dance in which performers in a lion costume mimic a lion's movements for entertainment and to bring good fortune (English Wikipedia). It is normally performed by two dancers (head and tail) to vigorous drums, gongs and cymbals, with fundamental movements drawn from Chinese martial arts. The two main forms are the Northern Lion and Southern Lion; the lion was likely introduced via Central Asia.
lion-dance.insight: A centuries-old emblem of Chinese folk culture spread worldwide by the diaspora, performed at New Year, openings and celebrations to chase away evil and bring luck (English Wikipedia; New World Encyclopedia).

buchaechum.name: Buchaechum (Fan dance)
buchaechum.tagline: Korean fan dance with peony-painted folding fans
buchaechum.profile: Buchaechum is a neoclassical Korean fan dance usually performed by groups of female dancers who manipulate large folding fans painted with pink peony blossoms to create flowing formations representing birds, flowers, butterflies, dragons and waves (Wikipedia). Dancers wear brightly coloured hanbok and perform to minyo (folk song) or sanjo (instrumental solo) accompaniment. It was created in 1954 by dancer Kim Baek-bong, who drew on Korean shamanic ritual dances and Joseon court and folk dances; it is therefore a modern, not ancient, creation.
buchaechum.insight: Buchaechum gained international prominence when a Korean folk-dance troupe performed it at the 1968 Summer Olympics in Mexico City; in 1993 the Korea Dance Association designated Buchaechum a masterpiece, and on 15 October 2014 it was registered as the third intangible cultural property of South Pyongan Province (Wikipedia; Korea.net).

apsara-dance.name: Apsara Dance
apsara-dance.era: Imagery from the Angkor period; modern form created 1940s–50s
apsara-dance.tagline: Cambodia's celestial-nymph dance of curling fingers
apsara-dance.profile: The Apsara dance (Robam Apsara) is a classical Khmer dance portraying apsaras — celestial nymphs of Hindu and Buddhist legend — known for slow, graceful movements and intricate, hyper-flexible finger and hand gestures, performed in golden costumes and headdresses modeled on the bas-reliefs of Angkor Wat (Royal Ballet of Cambodia, Wikipedia; Aurora Travel). The modern form was created under Queen Sisowath Kossamak in the 1940s–50s, with her granddaughter Princess Norodom Buppha Devi as the first principal Apsara dancer.
apsara-dance.insight: Apsara dance is the best-known piece of the Royal Ballet of Cambodia, which UNESCO proclaimed a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity in 2003 (inscribed on the Representative List in 2008); the art nearly died under the Khmer Rouge and its revival became a symbol of Cambodian cultural rebirth.

legong.name: Legong
legong.tagline: Refined Balinese palace dance of celestial maidens
legong.profile: Legong is a refined classical Balinese dance that probably originated in the 19th century as royal court entertainment (Wikipedia; Britannica). Legend holds that a prince of Sukawati fell ill and dreamed of two maidens dancing to gamelan, and on recovering arranged for such dances to be performed. Traditionally danced by two pre-adolescent girls accompanied by a third attendant (condong), it is marked by intricate finger and hand gestures, rapid footwork and expressive darting eye movements (seledet). The classic Legong Keraton enacts the tale of the East Javanese King of Lasem from the Malat romances. By 1931 Legong had become a marketed tourist performance.
legong.insight: Legong is the proving ground for all genres of Balinese women's dance and is among the nine dances within the three Balinese genres inscribed by UNESCO in 2015 (Academia.edu; Jakarta Post).

saman.name: Saman
saman.era: Roots attributed to 13th century; developed by Syekh Saman
saman.tagline: Gayo seated dance of synchronized claps and Islamic verse
saman.profile: The Saman is a seated dance of the Gayo people of Aceh province, Sumatra (UNESCO; Wikipedia). Boys and young men kneel in tight rows and clap their hands, slap their chests, thighs and the ground, click their fingers and sway and twist in time with a shifting rhythm, with no musical instruments. The sung verses - in the Gayo language - offer religious, romantic or humorous guidance and were historically a medium of Islamic preaching (dakwah) developed by Syekh Saman. A leader called the syekh directs the movements. Performances cement relationships between villages who invite each other to perform.
saman.insight: Saman was inscribed on UNESCO's List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in Need of Urgent Safeguarding on 24 November 2011 (6.COM, Bali), with UNESCO noting weakening transmission as knowledgeable elders age without successors (UNESCO; ANTARA).

adumu.name: Adumu (Maasai jumping dance)
adumu.tagline: Maasai warriors' competitive vertical jumping dance
adumu.profile: Adumu (from the Maa verb meaning 'to jump') is the Maasai jumping dance performed by young warriors (morani) of Kenya and Tanzania (Wikipedia). It forms part of the Eunoto coming-of-age ceremony, which usually involves ten or more days of singing, dancing and rituals as junior warriors transition to senior-warrior status (Jacada Travel). Dancers form a circle and take turns leaping straight up with a stiff posture, heels never touching the ground, while companions raise the pitch of their chant in time with the height of each jump (Wikipedia; Jacada Travel).
adumu.insight: The height and grace of a warrior's leap signals strength and desirability to onlooking young women, making Adumu both a display of physical prowess and a courtship element within the Eunoto rite (Lughayangu; African Safaris).

sabar.name: Sabar
sabar.tagline: Senegal's Wolof drum dance — the high-leaping, hip-driving, machine-gun sabar drum's signature dance, the soul of Dakar street celebrations.
sabar.profile: The sabar is a traditional drum from Senegal that is also played in Mauritania, The Gambia. It is associated with Wolof and Serer people. The drum is generally played with one hand and one stick or "galan". There are many different kinds of sabar, each with a different sound and a different role in the ensemble. Some common forms of sabar are n'der, thiol, goron, m'beng m'beng, toungoné, and xiin. The sabar is made from the wood of the dimb tree from the Senegambia region. The drums are carved by the laobé, or carvers, and generally skinned by the griot.
sabar.insight: Sabar drum rhythms function as a coded language — each rhythm has a specific name and contextual meaning, with master drummers (gewel) able to 'speak' through their drums to communicate praise, criticism, or family history to specific dancers in the circle. The tradition is maintained by hereditary griot lineages that trace their drum-knowledge back over 700 years, making sabar one of the world's longest-documented continuous percussion traditions.

kuduro.name: Kuduro
kuduro.tagline: Angola's frenetic electronic street dance of survival and joy
kuduro.profile: Kuduro is a high-energy Angolan electronic dance and music style that took shape in Luanda from the late 1980s into the 1990s, combining traditional Angolan semba with Western house and techno (Music of Angola, Wikipedia). It is danced at roughly 140 beats per minute with fast, stiff, often acrobatic footwork, hip thrusts and rapid arm gestures. Tony Amado is credited with naming and popularizing it, reportedly inspired by a stiff bar-dance scene in the film Kickboxer; the dance came before the music (FIELD journal; NPR).
kuduro.insight: Born during a brutal civil war, kuduro became, in scholar Marissa Moorman's framing via NPR, "a story of triumph over bone-crushing conditions" — young men in Luanda's musseques turned hardship into a defiant celebration of being alive, and the style later went global through acts like Buraka Som Sistema.

otea.name: Otea
otea.tagline: Fast hip-shaking Tahitian group dance to drums.
otea.profile: The oteea is a percussion-driven group dance with rapid hip motion, danced in several rows. Once a male warrior dance, it now has male (oteea tane), female (oteea vahine) and mixed (oteea amui) forms. Dancers execute figures (tamau, varu, otamu, ami, faarapu) while gesturing daily-life, nature or warfare themes. Accompaniment is drums only - the toere slit-log drum, the sharkskin pahu, and the smaller faatete - with no singing. Costumes use long plant-fiber (more) skirts with tassels and elaborate headpieces (English Wikipedia; Air Tahiti Nui).
otea.insight: Considered Tahiti's most spectacular dance; its modern choreography was standardized when Madeleine Moua founded the Heiva troupe in 1956 (English Wikipedia).

khaleegi.name: Khaleegi
khaleegi.tagline: The Gulf women's hair dance — the thobe twirls, the hair flies, the rhythm is shoulder and hip in equal measure.
khaleegi.profile: Khaleeji (Arabic: خليجي), may refer to: The native Arabs from the Arab states of the Persian Gulf, especially those from the Gulf Cooperation Council states Culture of Eastern Arabia, associated with Arab states of the Persian Gulf Gulf Arabic, a dialect of the Arabic language spoken in Eastern Arabia's coast of the Persian Gulf Khaliji (music), a type of music from Eastern Arabia (Arab states of the Persian Gulf) Khaleeji (currency), an idea for a common currency for the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) member states Khaleegy (dance), a traditional dance from the Persian Gulf countries Kaligi p…
khaleegi.insight: Khaleegi is danced almost exclusively at women-only gatherings across the Arabian Peninsula — weddings, henna ceremonies, family celebrations — where women remove their abayas to reveal the brilliantly embroidered thobe al-nashal underneath. The dance's signature hair-flipping section is performed only in the privacy of these women's spaces, making the khaleegi one of the few dances where the most virtuosic moments are reserved for an internal audience by cultural design.

jatjatin-dance.name: Jatjatin Dance
jatjatin-dance.tagline: A monsoon duet of separation and a midnight ritual for rain in the Mithila region.
jatjatin-dance.profile: Jatjatin is a traditional folk dance originating from the Mithila region, which spans northern Bihar in India and southern Nepal. It is primarily recognized as a duet between a man and a woman that dramatizes the emotional toll of seasonal labor migration. The performance captures the moment a husband prepares to leave for work while his wife expresses her sorrow through symbolic movement. Beyond its narrative form, the dance serves a critical ritual function during periods of drought as a plea for divine intervention.
jatjatin-dance.insight: During droughts, women perform this dance at midnight while chanting Vedic mantras to summon Lord Indra, the god of rain, to end agricultural crises.
sources: Source: Jatjatin Dance on Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jatjatin_Dance

jatjatin-dance.profile_long:
The Jatjatin dance is a cultural cornerstone of the Mithila region, a territory defined by its shared linguistic and social traditions across the border of India and Nepal. The dance exists in two primary contexts: as a narrative folk performance and as a sacred ritual. In its narrative form, it is typically performed during the monsoon season, a time when the agricultural cycle often dictates the movement of people. The dance portrays a couple facing the reality of separation as the man prepares to depart for employment elsewhere. The woman’s movements are characterized by the fluttering of her dupatta, which serves as a visual metaphor for tears and emotional distress, while the man’s presence provides the counterpoint of necessity and departure.

When the monsoon rains fail, the Jatjatin takes on a more urgent, sacred character. In these instances of agricultural crisis, the performance shifts from a daytime or evening entertainment to a midnight ritual conducted by women. This version of the dance is integrated with the chanting of Vedic mantras and traditional worship ceremonies aimed specifically at Lord Indra, the deity associated with rain and storms. The community believes that the collective energy of the dance and the sincerity of the songs can appease the god and bring an end to the drought. This dual nature of the Jatjatin—both a reflection of human relationships and a tool for environmental survival—highlights its deep integration into the Mithila way of life.

The music accompanying the Jatjatin is provided by the dholak, a double-headed drum, and the manjira, small hand cymbals. These instruments provide a steady rhythmic foundation for the circular footwork that defines the dance’s physical structure. The lyrics of the Jat-Jatin songs are often plaintive, focusing on themes of resilience and the pain of parting. Despite the sorrowful themes, the dance is a communal event that reinforces social bonds and provides a structured way for the community to process both personal grief and collective anxiety over the harvest.

images.attribution: Ramesh Lalwani / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY 2.0
images.description: Jat Jatin is the dance of women of the Mithila region of Bihar and is supposed to be performed on moonlit nights during the monsoons. Grown-up girls and young housewives assemble in the courtyard and, accompanied by a drum, dance from midnight to dawn. As they dance, they enact in gestures the epic story of the love of Jata and Jatin. The most dramatic episode of the dance concerns a wicked boatma

jatjatin-dance.sacred_note: When performed as a ritual for rain, the dance is held at midnight and involves the chanting of Vedic mantras and traditional worship ceremonies to Lord Indra.

puxada-de-rede.name: Puxada de Rede
puxada-de-rede.tagline: Bahian fishermen's dramatic net-pulling dance honoring Iemanja.
puxada-de-rede.profile: Puxada de rede ('pulling of the net') is a Brazilian folkloric theatrical dance from Bahia/the Northeast, often performed within capoeira shows. Based on a legend of a fisherman who drowns at sea and whose body is found in the net, it dramatizes the labor and grief of traditional xareu net-fishing and invokes Iemanja, goddess of the sea. Danced to a slow atabaque beat with songs and synchronized net-pulling movements; families sing and clap on the beach (English Wikipedia; Mandingueira).
puxada-de-rede.insight: The tradition is rooted in the post-slavery period when freed people turned to artisanal fishing in Santo Amaro, Bahia; the artisanal practice has declined since the 1970s (English Wikipedia).

yarkhushta.name: Yarkhushta
yarkhushta.profile: Yarkhushta (Յարխուշտա) is an Armenian folk and martial dance associated with the highlands of historic Sasun in Western Armenia, belonging to the category of Armenian "clap dances" (tsap parer). Men face one another in pairs, rapidly approach and vigorously clap the palms of the opposite dancer (Wikipedia). It is mentioned in the works of Movses Khorenatsi, Faustus of Byzantium and Grigor Magistros, indicating early-medieval origins, and was traditionally danced by soldiers before combat to cast off fear.
yarkhushta.insight: The dance's loud zurna and deep bass-drum pairing produces a wide peak-to-peak sound amplitude that can place dancers in a euphoric, adrenaline-fueled trance; revived by the Maratuk and Karin ensembles, there have been efforts to introduce it into the Armenian Army's repertoire (Wikipedia).

kochari.name: Kochari
kochari.era: Ancient; over 1,000 years of attested practice
kochari.tagline: Ancient ram-leaping circle dance of shared identity
kochari.profile: Kochari (Քոչարի) is a traditional Armenian group folk dance from the Armenian highlands, performed in lines or semicircles with dancers holding hands or shoulders, featuring energetic knee bends and leaps that imitate horned animals; in Armenian the name means roughly "knee-come" (Wikipedia; UNESCO). It is danced by men and women of all ages to zurna and dhol, with a tempo ranging from moderate to fast and a lead dancer signalling figure changes.
kochari.insight: Kochari was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity on December 6, 2017 (decision 12.COM 11.b.2, Jeju, South Korea); UNESCO notes it "provides a sense of shared identity and solidarity" and is "one of the rare traditional dances whose chain of transmission has never been interrupted."

armenian-dance.name: Armenian dance
armenian-dance.tagline: One of the world's oldest, most varied dance heritages
armenian-dance.profile: Armenian dance (Հայկական պար, bar) is considered one of the oldest and most varied dance traditions of its region, with rock paintings of country dancing in the Armenian highlands dating from the fifth to third millennia BC (Wikipedia). Dances are typically circle or line forms accompanied by folk instruments — the duduk, zurna and dhol — and traditional taraz costume. The repertoire ranges from ritual and military dances to wedding, solo and duet forms, historically divided by age and gender.
armenian-dance.insight: Composer Komitas observed that "dance expresses the typical characteristics of every nation, especially its traditions and degree of civilization"; Armenian dance has been successfully exported to international folk- and circle-dance communities and remains central to diaspora identity (Wikipedia; ArmGeo).

belly-dance.name: Belly dance
belly-dance.era: ancient roots; term coined 1860s; Egyptian classical form 20th century
belly-dance.tagline: Torso-driven dance of hip and abdomen articulations
belly-dance.profile: Belly dance is the Western name (from the French danse du ventre, coined in the 1860s) for a torso-driven dance emphasising articulations of the hips and torso, with Egypt's forms the most recognised worldwide. Per Wikipedia, in Egypt it has two contexts: the social/folk raqs baladi danced by ordinary people at celebrations, and the professional raqs sharqi of cabarets and film. It isolates the torso muscles rather than moving the limbs through space, distinguishing it from many Western dance forms.
belly-dance.insight: Belly dance is among the most globally widespread Middle Eastern dance forms, though it remains contested within parts of the Arab world; Egyptian cinema spread its imagery worldwide (Wikipedia).

punto-music.name: Punto music
punto-music.tagline: Spain — Hispanic musical genre which includes melodic and choreographic form
punto-music.profile: The Panamanian punto (Spanish: punto panameño or el punto) is a Hispanic musical genre which includes melodic and choreographic form. It has composition created specifically for dance, typically performed by a single couple as a demonstration of skill, precision and grace. Unlike the tamborito and the Panamanian cumbia, it is performed as an intermission between other dances or music at a party or event.
punto-music.insight: A striking difference from other dances of this type is that only men can move outside the circle.

agbekor.name: Agbekor
agbekor.tagline: Ewe and Fon war dance once known as Atamga ('great oath')
agbekor.profile: Agbekor is a music-and-dance form of the Ewe and Fon peoples of West Africa, an ancient dance once known as Atamga (Ga = 'great', Atam = 'oath'), now performed by the people of Dzogadze near Akatsi in the southern Volta Region of Ghana (Wikipedia). It is highly polyrhythmic in a 12/8 cycle anchored by the gankogui bell, with the atsimevu lead drum calling dancers to specific movements; it features slow and fast sections with interlude 'hatsiatsia' songs. Historically a war dance, the oath refers to one taken by ancestors before battle (Wikipedia).
agbekor.insight: Agbekor is now a cornerstone of West African drumming curricula worldwide, transmitted internationally by Ewe master drummers and documented through ethnomusicological transcriptions of bell timelines and drum parts (Melodigging).

agbadza.name: Agbadza
agbadza.era: Derived from war dance Atrikpui; recreational form c. 1920s
agbadza.tagline: Ewe recreational dance evolved from the Atrikpui war dance
agbadza.profile: Agbadza is among the oldest musical types of the Southern Ewe of Ghana, Togo, Benin and parts of southwestern Nigeria, derived from the older war dance Atrikpui (Wikipedia; African Music Safari). As a social and recreational form it is open to all, and is performed at the Hogbetsotso festival, funerals and weddings. Performance has five sections: Banyinyi, Vutsortsor (main dance), Adzo, Hatsatsa (song cycle) and a final Vutsortsor, driven by the Sogo lead drum, kidi, gankogui bell and axatse rattle (Wikipedia).
agbadza.insight: Ethnomusicologist David Locke of Tufts University has published critical-edition transcriptions of Agbadza drumming, and Ewe master drummer Gideon Foli Alorwoyie featured it in 1960s folkloric groups (Wikipedia).

afro-fusion.name: Afro fusion
afro-fusion.tagline: dance and musical style that emerged between the 1970s and 2000s
afro-fusion.profile: Afro fusion (also spelled afrofusion or afro-fusion) is a dance and musical style that emerged between the 1970s and 2000s. In the same way as the dance style, the musical style invokes fusions of various regional and inter-continental musical cultures, such as jazz, hip hop, kwaito, reggae, soul, pop, kwela, blues, folk, rock and afrobeat.

assiko.name: Assiko
assiko.tagline: Bassa guitar-and-bottle dance of hip-driven footwork
assiko.profile: Assiko is a popular dance and music style of the Bassa people of southern Cameroon, its name from "Assi" (earth/ground) and "Ko" (foot) (Wikipedia; African Music Library). Danced in a T-shirt and full, billowing skirt that emphasizes hip movement, its choreography uses lop-sided, gliding walks at varying heights — standing or crouching — with feats of balance and contortion. Musically it pairs a singer and guitarist with a percussionist striking an empty bottle with metal knives and forks for its crisp, metallic rhythm.
assiko.insight: Assiko gained popularity around the 1920s, spreading from Bassa villages to Douala and Yaoundé and beyond Cameroon; Jean Bikoko "Aladin" is regarded as the father of modern assiko and one of Central Africa's finest, under-recognized guitar masters (African Music Library).

bitti-harey.profile: Bitti Harey is a traditional dance of the Zarma people especially that of Zarmaganda in Niger. It is part of the traditional dance to celebrate the end of a good harvest, festivals, wrestling matches and weddings Bitti Harey is rooted in the cultural tradition of the Zarmaganda. The handling of the elements that make up the instrumental ensemble of Bitti Harey is handled by seasoned actors with perfect knowledge of the rhythm. The word "Bitti Harey" literally translates into "drum rhythm".

ambasse-bey.tagline: Germany — style of folk music and dance from Cameroon
ambasse-bey.profile: Ambasse bey or ambas-i-bay is a style of folk music and dance from Cameroon. The music is based on commonly available instruments, especially guitar, with percussion provided by sticks and bottles. The music is faster-paced than assiko. John Hall described its rhythm as the one of a moving broom. Where dancers swing their shoulders like the wings of birds, the dance is composed of sequences of fluid steps and jerky body movements performed in accordance with the music, which is generally the makossa. In order to perform this dance, the dancers must wear traditional sawa outfits.
ambasse-bey.insight: According to several contemporaries, the Ambass Bey was first taught in Douala by the Dayas family, notably Joseph Dayas and Engom'a Dayas at Bonadouma Home.

The performers form a circle and follow each other, taking steps forward and backward; the dance is punctuated by the ngôma ensemble (several double-skin drums). Previously the macheve cowbells that the dancers wore on their feet participated as musical instruments.

coladeira.tagline: Cape Verde — morna's faster, brighter sister. Joy where morna had longing. Created in the 1950s to make people laugh.
coladeira.profile: The coladeira (Local Portuguese pronunciation: [kulɐˈdejɾɐ]; Kabuverdianu: koladera, [kolɐˈdeɾɐ]) is a music genre from Cape Verde. It is characterized by a variable tempo, a 2-beat bar, and (in its most traditional form) a harmonic structure based in a cycle of fifths. The lyrics structure is organized in strophes that alternate with a refrain. The tone is generally joyful and themes often include social criticism. Instrumentation typically includes a guitar, a cavaquinho, and percussion, among others.
coladeira.insight: This is followed by the same movement to the other side: the right foot moves back to the right with a weigh-shift to the right foot, and the left foot comes back to tap beside the right also invented and mastered by Tommy Andrade in 1995 from Brockton.

djol.tagline: mask-dance from Temine people in Sierra Leone
djol.profile: Djolé (also known as Jolé or Yolé) is a mask-dance from Temine people in Sierra Leone. It is played traditionally with a large square drum called sikko. Although a mask depicts a female, it is carried by a male. Djolé is played usually during big feasts which involve many villages to celebrate a good harvest, the end of the Ramadan or a marriage. Nowadays the rhythm has been rearranged to be played with the djembé and is very popular in particular in Guinea.
djol.insight: Djolé (also known as Jolé or Yolé) is a mask-dance from Temine people in Sierra Leone.

eskista.name: Eskista
eskista.era: ancient (traced by some to the Axumite era)
eskista.profile: Eskista (Amharic for 'dancing shoulders') is a traditional dance of the Amhara of Ethiopia, also strongly associated with Tigray. Per Wikipedia, it is built on rapid, rhythmic rolling and bouncing of the shoulders plus chest and neck movements, performed to traditional instruments such as the masinqo (one-string fiddle), krar (lyre) and kebero (drum). A staple of weddings and festivals, it often features shilimat, where admirers stick money to the best dancer's forehead. Folklore links its snake-like neck motion to mimicking a serpent.
eskista.insight: Considered one of the most technically demanding African dances, eskista is Ethiopia's most iconic dance and has gone global (Wikipedia; Lakewood Center for the Arts).

chakacha.name: Chakacha
chakacha.tagline: Swahili coastal women's hip-driven wedding dance
chakacha.profile: Chakacha is a traditional music and dance style (a ngoma) of the Swahili people of coastal Kenya and Tanzania, originally associated with weddings and traditionally performed and watched by women (Wikipedia). The hip-swaying movement, danced with a belt tied at the waist for ease of movement, bears resemblance to Middle Eastern belly dance, reflecting centuries of Arab and Persian trade influence on the Swahili coast. It shares music and Swahili lyrics with taarab and uses a twelve-beat triplet rhythm.
chakacha.insight: In the late 20th century bands such as Mombasa Roots, Safari Sound Band and Them Mushrooms adapted chakacha into popular Afropop, carrying the once women-only wedding genre onto commercial recordings (Wikipedia).

The dance is characterised by fancy footwork and galloping body movements in the style of racing horses. The dance was popularized by members of the Khiama Boyz, including Macheso, Madzibaba, and Tazvida.

goli.name: Goli
goli.era: adopted by the Baoule c.1900-1910 (originally from the Wan people)
goli.tagline: Day-long Baoule masquerade of four sacred mask pairs
goli.profile: Goli is a day-long masquerade dance of the Baoule people of central Cote d'Ivoire, adopted from their Wan neighbours around 1900-1910. Per the Metropolitan Museum of Art and Wikipedia, two dancers wear four mask types in a fixed order: the disc-shaped kple kple, the horned animal helmet goli glin, the ram-horned kpan pre and the human-faced kpan. Masks appear in male/female pairs and embody bush spirits; the event, accompanied by drums and palm wine, is staged for the funerals of notables and for entertainment, and is believed to protect the village.
goli.insight: Goli has become the dominant Baoule dance, gradually displacing older forms, and its kple kple disc mask is among the most recognised of all African mask forms (Metropolitan Museum of Art; Wikipedia).

diski-dance.name: Diski Dance
diski-dance.tagline: South Africa, 2010 — dance composed of a series of choreographed football moves, named from different parts of the country, and …
diski-dance.profile: The Diski Dance is a dance composed of a series of choreographed football moves, named from different parts of the country, and was created for the 2010 FIFA World Cup as part of its advertising campaign. The creator of the Diski Dance was South African choreographer Wendy Ramokgadi, who died on Friday 27 May 2011. The moves are named in Tswana, Zulu, Sotho and English amongst others and include "Tsamaya", "Heel Extension Mkhari" and "Chester". The adverts were shown on CNN, BBC, Eurosport and SkySports amongst others.
diski-dance.insight: The Diski dance was featured in Matt Harding's 2010 "Where the Hell is Matt in South Africa?

fanga.name: Fanga
fanga.tagline: Nigeria, 1943 — dance "interpretation of a traditional Liberian invocation to the earth and sky"
fanga.profile: Fanga is a dance "interpretation of a traditional Liberian invocation to the earth and sky". The dance originated in Liberia or Sierra Leone. The first performance of a version of Fanga in the United States may have been by Asadata Dafora in 1943; Marcia Ethel Heard believes that Pearl Primus hid Dafora's influence on her work. The dance was written by Primus in 1959 in conjunction with the National Dance Company of Liberia.
fanga.insight: Babatunde Olatunji described Fanga as a dance of welcome from Liberia and he, and many others, used a song created by LaRocque Bey to go with the rhythm and dance, assisted by some of the students in his Harlem studio, during the early 1960s.

gurewol.name: Guérewol
gurewol.profile: The Guérewol (var. Guerewol, Gerewol) is an annual courtship ritual competition among the Wodaabe Fula people of Niger. Young men dressed in elaborate ornamentation and made up in traditional face painting gather in lines to dance and sing, vying for the attentions of marriageable young women. The Guérewol occurs each year as the traditionally nomadic Wodaabe cattle herders gather at the southern edge of the Sahara before dispersing south on their dry season pastures.

kwassa-kwassa.tagline: Hips back-and-forth, hands following - the soukous craze
kwassa-kwassa.profile: Kwassa kwassa is a Congolese (DR Congo) dance and the fast soukous style it accompanies, emerging in the 1980s. Per Wikipedia, the dance was created by Jeanora, a Kinshasa mechanic, who mimicked the motion of a gearshift; the hips move back and forth while the hands follow the hips. It was globally popularised through the music videos of Paris-based soukous star Kanda Bongo Man, who restructured soukous with guitar solos after every verse rather than only at the song's end.
kwassa-kwassa.insight: Kwassa kwassa carried Congolese soukous to dancefloors across Africa and the diaspora in the late 1980s, and the term later entered global pop culture (Wikipedia; African Music Library).

indlamu.name: Indlamu
indlamu.tagline: Zulu's high-kick warrior dance — the leg lifted vertical, the foot stamped to the ground with thunder, shield and spear in hand.
indlamu.profile: Indlamu (Zulu pronunciation: [ind͡ɮaːmu], Afrikaans: Zoeloedans) is a traditional Zulu dance from Southern Africa, synonymous with the Zulu tribe of South Africa and the Northern Ndebele tribe of Western Zimbabwe. The dance began as a war dance during the reign of King Shaka. The dance is characterised by the dancer lifting one foot over his/her head and bringing it down sharply, landing squarely on the downbeat. Typically, two dancers in warrior's pelts perform indlamu routines together, shadowing each other's moves perfectly.
indlamu.insight: Indlamu's signature foot-strike is so percussive that warriors can break the ground at the point of impact — a dance feat that has been documented at every King Shaka Day celebration in KwaZulu-Natal. The dance is now recognised by the South African government as a national cultural heritage, and the annual Royal Reed Dance at the Zulu king's residence at eNyokeni Palace draws over 25,000 young women and warriors each September.

malipenga.profile: Malipenga is an African dance music of the Tonga people of Malawi. The dance was originated in imitations of military drills when they fought alongside the British Army in World War I. Malipenga is common in the central and northern regions of Malawi, as in Tanzania, Mozambique, and Zambia with slight modifications. Each year in August is held a big Malipenga festival in Northern Malawi in a different town each year.

mopacho.name: Mopacho
mopacho.profile: Mopacho is a Congolese full-body dance that, per French Wikipedia, was created in Ouenze in the 5th arrondissement of Brazzaville by Zagala Mboyo, alias Sixte Singha, in 1990, inspired by the Mbochi dances of Boundji (Cuvette department). It engages the head, neck, shoulders, torso, hips and limbs in continuous motion - arms crossed in an 'X,' gentle hip rotations and a gradually lowering pelvis. It went viral in the early 2020s via TikTok, especially after DJ Afara Tsena's 2022 hit 'Afro Mbokalisation,' and was adopted by stars such as Fally Ipupa, Serge Beynaud and Gaz Mawete.
mopacho.insight: Often described as 'sculpture in motion,' mopacho became a defining viral dance of Francophone Africa in 2024 and a point of Congolese cultural pride, prompting a national competition (Wikipedia; Afrocritik).

muchongoyo-dance.name: Muchongoyo dance
muchongoyo-dance.tagline: presentational dance and drumming style that emphasizes acrobatic and stomping sequences to dazzle spectato…
muchongoyo-dance.profile: Muchongoyo is a presentational dance and drumming style that emphasizes acrobatic and stomping sequences to dazzle spectators during gatherings or competitions with a complementary rythme of sharp claps. In Zimbabwe, it is the most well-liked Ndau dance. In Zimbabwe's Chipinge, Chimanimani, Chiredzi, and Buhera districts, muchongoyo is a traditional dance that is performed for celebratory purposes or events of cultural significance such as burials of chief and royals. It particularly identifies with the Ndau people, though less strongly identifies with the Tsonga (Shangani) people.
muchongoyo-dance.insight: Around 2010, the two galas were on their way out.

mbende-jerusarema-dance.tagline: prominent dance style among the Zezuru Shona of eastern Zimbabwe, particularly in the Murewa and Uzumba-Mar…
mbende-jerusarema-dance.profile: Mbende Jerusarema dance is a prominent dance style among the Zezuru Shona of eastern Zimbabwe, particularly in the Murewa and Uzumba-Maramba-Pfungwe districts. Traditional dances and performances, such as Jerusarema, are still vital living traditions in Zimbabwe, performed in a variety of settings and respected by local communities. Traditional dances are done for a variety of reasons, including entertainment, ritual, festivals, and memorial and celebration. The Shona used Jerusarema as a battle dance and a diversionary technique during military encounters, according to popular belief.
