morris-dance.name: Morris Dance
morris-dance.tagline: England's bell-jingling village ritual dance — handkerchiefs, sticks, white clothes, blackened faces, bells at the knees; the spring fertility tradition that refuses to die.
morris-dance.profile: Morris dance is the centuries-old ritual folk dance of the English villages — earliest written records date to the 15th century — performed by costumed troupes (sides) wearing white shirts and trousers with bells strapped to their shins. Dancers move in formation around a leader, sometimes carrying handkerchiefs to wave, sometimes striking wooden sticks together in synchronized patterns. Multiple regional traditions survive: Cotswold morris (the most familiar), Border morris (darker, more theatrical), Long Sword and Rapper morris (with metal swords), and the women's Northwest morris from Lancashire. Morris is performed each May 1st (May Day) by surviving sides across England.
morris-dance.insight: Morris dancing has been performed continuously in some English villages for over 500 years — the Bampton Morris in Oxfordshire claims an unbroken tradition since the 1500s, danced every Whit Monday since records began. The English Folk Dance and Song Society (founded by Cecil Sharp in 1911) saved morris from extinction in the early 20th century by documenting every surviving village tradition; today around 800 morris sides perform across England, the United States, and Australia.

maypole.name: Maypole Dance
maypole.tagline: The Northern European spring rite — dancers weave coloured ribbons around the maypole, an unbroken pre-Christian ritual now embraced from Stockholm to Wellington.
maypole.profile: The maypole dance is the pre-Christian Northern European spring ritual where dancers — each holding a coloured ribbon attached to the top of a tall pole — weave in and out of formation in opposite directions, braiding the ribbons into geometric patterns down the pole's length. The tradition is most strongly maintained in Sweden (where Midsummer's Eve in late June is the national high holiday and the maypole — majstång — is raised in every village), Germany, England, and the Czech Republic. The maypole survives wherever Northern European descendants settled — the German diaspora in Texas, the English in Australia and New Zealand, the Swedes in Minnesota.
maypole.insight: Sweden's Midsommarafton — Midsummer's Eve — is the country's most widely celebrated national holiday, when virtually every Swedish village raises its majstång (maypole) and the population dances the small frogs dance (Små Grodorna) around it. The combination of summer-solstice daylight (the sun barely sets in central Sweden in late June) and centuries-old ritual makes Swedish Midsummer one of the most photographed traditional celebrations in Europe.

kalbelia.name: Kalbelia
kalbelia.tagline: Rajasthani snake-charmer community's serpentine women's dance
kalbelia.profile: Kalbelia is the song-and-dance tradition of the Kalbelia (Kabeliya) community of Rajasthan, formerly professional snake handlers (UNESCO). Women in flowing black skirts dance and swirl, replicating the movements of a serpent, while men accompany on the khanjari percussion and the poongi, a woodwind traditionally used to charm snakes (UNESCO). Dancers wear traditional tattoos, jewellery and garments embroidered with mirrors and silver thread; songs convey mythological stories and are improvised, transmitted orally without written texts (UNESCO).
kalbelia.insight: Kalbelia folk songs and dances of Rajasthan were inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2010, and dancer Gulabo Sapera is among its best-known exponents (UNESCO/Indian Culture).

lavani.name: Lavani
lavani.era: Traceable to the 1560s; flourished under Peshwa rule (18th-19th c)
lavani.profile: Lavani is a popular genre of song and dance from Maharashtra, combining traditional song with dance performed to the beats of the dholki drum and noted for its powerful rhythm (Wikipedia). Female performers wear nine-yard nauvari saris and dance to quick-tempo songs that address society, religion, politics and romance, often with erotic or satirical overtones (Wikipedia). It has two main streams - the philosophical Nirguni Lavani and the sensual Shringari Lavani - and developed into public Phadachi Lavani and intimate Baithakichi Lavani; it has been central to Marathi folk theatre (tamasha) (Wikipedia).
lavani.insight: Patronized by Maratha lords and prominent during late Peshwa rule, Lavani originally served as entertainment and a morale-booster for soldiers, and many performers come from Maharashtra's Mahar, Kolhati and Matang communities (Wikipedia).

ghoomar.name: Ghoomar
ghoomar.era: Bhil tribal origins, later adopted by Rajputs
ghoomar.tagline: Rajasthani twirling veil-and-ghaghara women's folk dance
ghoomar.profile: Ghoomar is a traditional folk dance of Rajasthan originally performed by the Bhil tribe to worship the goddess Saraswati and later embraced by Rajput communities (Wikipedia). Chiefly performed by veiled women in flowing skirts (ghaghara), dancers pirouette while moving in and out of a wide circle; the word derives from 'ghoomna', meaning twirling (Wikipedia). Newly married brides are traditionally expected to dance ghoomar when welcomed to their marital home, and it features at weddings, Teej and religious occasions, with regional variations across Udaipur, Jodhpur and Kota-Bundi (Pratha).
ghoomar.insight: Ghoomar reached wide modern visibility through the song 'Ghoomar' in the 2017 Bollywood film Padmaavat, and the Gangaur Ghoomar Dance Academy was founded by Rajmata Goverdhan Kumari in 1986 to preserve the form (Wikipedia).

frevo.name: Frevo
frevo.profile: Frevo is a Brazilian music-and-dance form performed mainly during the Carnival of Recife, Pernambuco. Its fast, vigorous rhythm fuses marching music, Brazilian tango, polka, quadrille and classical pieces played by martial bands; the accompanying dance 'passo' draws on capoeira agility with over a hundred structured steps, high jumps and acrobatics, often with small colorful umbrellas. Inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List in 2012 (file 00603, 7.COM); IPHAN-registered 2007 (UNESCO; Paco do Frevo).
frevo.insight: UNESCO inscribed 'Frevo, performing arts of the Carnival of Recife' in 2012; National Frevo Day is 9 February (UNESCO).

coco.name: Coco
coco.tagline: Afro-Brazilian Northeastern stomping song-dance (coco de roda).
coco.profile: Coco is an African-influenced musical rhythm and dance from northeastern Brazil, especially Alagoas and Paraiba, performed in a circle (coco de roda) with call-and-response singing and stomping (often in wooden clogs). Instruments include ganza, surdo, pandeiro and triangle. Earliest cocos were work songs of Afro-Brazilians, including at Palmares, sung while breaking coconuts, and tied to communal house-building on clay floors (English Wikipedia; Encyclopedia.com).
coco.insight: Coco is also called embolada and appears under many regional names (coco de ganza, coco de zambe); Encyclopedia.com traces its earliest forms to Afro-Brazilian work songs of Palmares.

reng.name: Reng
reng.era: codified Qajar era (19th c.); older roots
reng.tagline: Lively 6/8 instrumental dance-piece closing Persian classical performances
reng.profile: Reng is the rhythmic instrumental dance-piece form of Persian classical music - a lively metric composition, almost always in 6/8, performed at the conclusion of a dastgah performance (Persian traditional music, Wikipedia). A typical classical suite proceeds through pishdaramad, chaharmezrab, avaz, tasnif and ends with a reng (Persian traditional music, Wikipedia). Each dastgah has its own characteristic reng; the piece may be improvised or composed for one or more instruments, and is the principal dance form in the radif repertoire (Center for Iranian Music). Historically the reng was accompanied by 'Persian court dance' (raghs-e darbari) (Nasehpour).
reng.insight: The reng underpins much of Persian solo improvisational dance; raqs-e tehrani and Persian classical dance are largely improvised to the 6/8 reng rhythm (Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Dance').

tumba-francesa.name: Tumba Francesa
tumba-francesa.profile: Tumba francesa ('French drum') is an Afro-Haitian-Cuban genre of dance, song and drumming brought to eastern Cuba (Oriente) by French colonists and their enslaved Haitians fleeing the Haitian Revolution. It fuses the kinetic vocabulary of French court ballroom dances with African drumming. Two main dance styles survive: the mason (a light parody of French ballroom dance) and the yuba (improvised, to rousing drum rhythms). Instruments include the cata idiophone, three single-headed tumbas, the tamborita and the chacha/maruga, with a compose leading call-and-response with female tumberas (English Wikipedia; UNESCO).
tumba-francesa.insight: Inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List in 2008 (file 00052), having originally been proclaimed a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity in 2003 (UNESCO).

theyyam.name: Theyyam
theyyam.tagline: North Malabar ritual where the performer becomes a god
theyyam.profile: Theyyam (Theyyattam/Kaliyattam) is a ritual worship tradition of North Malabar, Kerala - chiefly Kannur and Kasaragod districts - in which the performer ritually embodies a deity (Kerala Tourism). After extended ritual singing (thottam) and 8-10 hours of preparation, the placement of the sacred headgear (mudi) marks the deity's entry into the performer's body, after which devotees of all castes seek the Theyyam's blessing directly. Some 456 Theyyam types are documented. Performers are predominantly men of Scheduled Caste communities such as Malayan and Vannan; costumes feature towering mudi headgear, deep red-and-black natural face/body painting and skirts of palm fronds. The season runs roughly mid-October to late May (Wikipedia).
theyyam.insight: Theyyam is closely related to Tulu Nadu's Buta Kola - Buta Kola is sometimes described as the parent form from which Theyyam evolved - and is distinct from southern Kerala's Padayani (HandWiki; Kerala Tourism).

beijing-opera.name: Beijing Opera
beijing-opera.tagline: China's premier theatrical art blending song, mime, acrobatics and dance
beijing-opera.profile: Peking (Beijing) opera (京劇, Jīngjù) is the dominant form of Chinese opera, combining instrumental music, vocal performance, mime, martial arts, dance and acrobatics (English Wikipedia). It arose in Beijing in the mid-Qing dynasty and was fully developed by the mid-19th century, with four main role types: sheng, dan, jing and chou. It is not strictly a dance but contains substantial stylized dance and movement.
beijing-opera.insight: Inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2010 (ref RL/00418), it is regarded as one of China's cultural treasures (UNESCO/Wikidata).

talchum.name: Talchum
talchum.tagline: Korean masked dance-drama of satirical folk theatre
talchum.profile: Talchum is a Korean masked dance-drama that encompasses dance, music and theatre, in which an ensemble of six to ten musicians accompanies masked performers who humorously explore social issues through dramatic combinations of songs, dances, movements and dialogue (UNESCO). Caricatured everyday characters - apostate monks, decadent yangban nobles, shamans - convey criticism of social hierarchy and an appeal to equality. It requires no formal stage, and the audience contributes with cheers and jeers. Regional forms include Bongsan Talchum and Hahoe byeolsingut talnori.
talchum.insight: 'Talchum, mask dance drama in the Republic of Korea' was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List in 2022 - Korea's 22nd ICH element - with exactly thirteen regional mask-dance-drama types collectively inscribed; its focus on social criticism fuelled a large-scale revival among university students in the 1970s and 1980s (UNESCO; Google Arts & Culture/ICHCAP).

jarabe-tapatio.name: Jarabe Tapatío
jarabe-tapatio.era: Jalisco 19th century · Mexican national dance since 1924
jarabe-tapatio.tagline: The Mexican Hat Dance — Jalisco's courtship dance where the woman dances upon the man's discarded sombrero, declared the national dance in 1924.
jarabe-tapatio.profile: The Jarabe Tapatío — the Mexican Hat Dance — is the national dance of Mexico, codified in the early 19th century by the dancers of Jalisco state and proclaimed national heritage by the Mexican Ministry of Public Education in 1924. The dance is a courtship narrative in eight to twelve sequenced sections, performed by a couple in traditional charro (man) and china poblana (woman) costume. The climactic moment comes when the man throws his wide-brimmed sombrero to the floor and the woman, accepting his suit, dances atop it. The accompanying mariachi music — most famously the El Jarabe Tapatío composition — is recognised globally as the sound of Mexico.
jarabe-tapatio.insight: The Jarabe Tapatío was officially declared Mexico's national dance in 1924 by the Mexican Ministry of Public Education during the post-revolutionary cultural codification programme. The dance's signature climactic moment — when the woman dances on the man's discarded sombrero — became the visual emblem of Mexican identity worldwide, performed at every major Mexican state event from presidential inaugurations to Día de la Independencia and at the openings of Mexican cultural centres across the global Mexican diaspora.

ainu-dance.name: Ainu dance
ainu-dance.tagline: Indigenous Ainu circle and animal-mimicry dances honoring the kamuy
ainu-dance.profile: Traditional Ainu dance comprises the dances of the Ainu, an Indigenous people living mostly in Hokkaido in northern Japan, performed at ceremonies, banquets and cultural festivals (UNESCO). The traditional style involves a large circle of dancers with onlookers singing accompaniment without instruments; some dances imitate the calls and movements of animals or insects (such as the crane dance, sarorun rimse), others such as the sword and bow dances are rituals (UNESCO). Believing deities dwell in their surroundings, the Ainu use dance to worship and thank nature; it is central to the Iyomante ceremony, in which a bear's embodied deity is sent back to heaven (UNESCO). It was designated an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property in 1984 and inscribed by UNESCO in 2009 (Japan House London).
ainu-dance.insight: For the Ainu, dance reinforces their connection to the natural and religious world and, per UNESCO, provides a cultural link to other Arctic peoples of Russia and North America (UNESCO).

mongol-biyelgee.name: Mongol Biyelgee
mongol-biyelgee.profile: Performed half-sitting or cross-legged in the confined space of the ger; hand, shoulder and chest movements depict household labour and ethnic identity. Regarded as the forebear of Mongolian national dances; UNESCO Urgent Safeguarding because transmitters are mostly elderly.

mbende-jerusarema.name: Mbende Jerusarema
mbende-jerusarema.tagline: A vigorous Zezuru Shona fertility dance that survived colonial bans under a biblical name.
mbende-jerusarema.profile: The Mbende Jerusarema is a traditional dance practiced by the Zezuru Shona people in eastern Zimbabwe, particularly in the Murewa and Uzumba-Maramba-Pfungwe districts. Characterized by acrobatic waist-shaking, sensual hip motions, and intense pelvic thrusts, it combines elements of a fertility, battle, and hunting dance. Originally called 'Mbende' after a fast-running mouse or mole, the dance was renamed Jerusarema under missionary pressure to give it a religious connotation. Today, it remains a powerful symbol of national pride, performed at weddings, funerals, and official state events.
mbende-jerusarema.insight: Once banned by missionaries for its raw sexuality, this ancient Zezuru Shona mouse-and-mole dance survived by adopting the biblical name Jerusarema.
mbende-jerusarema.profile_long:
The Mbende Jerusarema dance is a prominent cultural tradition among the Zezuru Shona people of eastern Zimbabwe, specifically thriving within the Murewa and Uzumba-Maramba-Pfungwe districts. This ancient performance has traversed three distinct eras of Zimbabwean culture: the pre-colonial period before 1890, the colonial period from 1890 to 1980, and the post-colonial era from 1980 to the present day. Traditionally, the Zezuru community utilized Jerusarema for a variety of critical life events, including weddings, festivities, recreational competitions, funerals, and political meetings. Popular belief also holds that the Shona used the dance as a battle dance and a diversionary technique during military encounters, alongside its primary roles as a ritual fertility, hunting, and death dance.

The dance's original name, Mbende, translates to 'fast-running mouse' or 'mole', reflecting the animal's symbolism of rapidity, fertility, sexuality, and family. Rather than acting out a direct caricature, dancers project these animal traits through specific physical movements. Men frequently crouch while jerking both arms and forcefully kicking the ground with the right leg, mimicking a tunneling mole casting soil to the surface. Meanwhile, women engage in seductive, acrobatic waist-shaking and hip motions in sync with the men, culminating in intense pelvic thrusts directed toward each other that electrify the audience.

During the colonial era, Christian missionaries severely disapproved of the dance, mistaking its powerful pelvic movements for sexually graphic and suggestive behavior. Seeking to suppress it, the missionaries worked with village chiefs and local authorities to prohibit the dance in the early 20th century. However, village chiefs successfully petitioned to preserve the performance by renaming it Jerusarema—derived from the Shona adaptation of Jerusalem—to grant it a religious connotation associated with the birth of Jesus Christ. Despite this veneer of scripture, the dance retained its core identity and served as a powerful source of pride and resistance against colonial power. In 2005, UNESCO proclaimed the Mbende Jerusarema a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity, followed by its inscription on the Representative List in 2008.

The auditory foundation of Mbende Jerusarema relies on a distinctive, polyrhythmic instrumentation that features no lyrics or singing. One master drummer—such as noted master percussionist Douglas Vembe—drives the rhythm using the mutumba drum, carved from the hard, resonant wood of the mutiti (Erythrina abyssinica) or mutsvanzwa (Pseudolachnostylis maprouneifolia) tree. This primary drum is accompanied by men playing wooden clappers (maja or manja) crafted from the durable mutara tree (Gardenia spathulifolia), alongside women handclapping, yodelling, and blowing whistles and rattles.

Material culture remains central to the tradition, particularly regarding clothing and instruments. Traditionally, dancers wore outfits made from the flexible, comfortable hides of wild animals such as leopards, monkeys, cheetahs, and wild cats, though modern practitioners increasingly blend textile fabrics with animal skins. Today, while the dance continues to be fiercely protected and practiced in rural clubs and urban gatherings, it faces new modern challenges. Its commercialization for tourist audiences and adaptation for official political rallies have occasionally stripped it of its traditional context, leading to the use of inferior instruments and altered meanings. Nevertheless, Mbende Jerusarema endures as an iconic pillar of Zimbabwean heritage.

gule-wamkulu.name: Gule Wamkulu
gule-wamkulu.tagline: Chewa Nyau masked spirit dance of the dead
gule-wamkulu.profile: Gule Wamkulu ('the great dance') is the masked ritual dance of the Chewa Nyau brotherhood, a secret society of initiated men in Malawi, Zambia and Mozambique (UNESCO ICH; Britannica). Performed at funerals, initiations (chinamwali), the installation or death of chiefs, and after the July harvest, dancers in wood-and-straw masks and costumes embody zilombo - spirits of the dead and wild animals (antelope, lions) as well as figures like slave traders and even helicopters - each character teaching moral and social lessons (UNESCO ICH; Nyau, Wikipedia). It dates to the 17th-century Chewa Empire.
gule-wamkulu.insight: Within the Chewa's matrilineal society the Nyau gave married men solidarity and authority; the masked dancers are regarded as actual spirits, not men, and must not be named as such. UNESCO proclaimed Gule Wamkulu a Masterpiece in 2005 and inscribed it in 2008 (UNESCO ICH).

isukuti.name: Isukuti
isukuti.tagline: Luhya drum dance, UNESCO urgent-safeguarding heritage
isukuti.profile: Isukuti is a fast-paced, energetic celebratory dance of the Isukha and Idakho communities (Luhya) of Western Kenya, accompanied by drumming and singing (UNESCO). The dance derives its name from the isukuti drums, played in sets of three (big, medium and small) and accompanied by an antelope horn and metal rattles; a soloist leads thematic songs as dancers form separate rows for men and women. It permeates childbirths, initiations, weddings, funerals, inaugurations and religious festivities.
isukuti.insight: In 2014 UNESCO inscribed the Isukuti dance on the List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in Need of Urgent Safeguarding, warning that transmission is weakening as bearers age and younger generations turn to more commercial genres (UNESCO).

currulao.name: Currulao
currulao.profile: An Afro-descendant marimba dance-music of Colombia's South Pacific coast (Choco, Valle del Cauca, Cauca, Narino) and Ecuador's Esmeraldas, in 6/8 with interlocking polyrhythms and call-and-response vocals (Smithsonian Folklife; Music of Colombia, Wikipedia). The ensemble centers on the marimba de chonta, cununo drums, bombo and guasa shaker; a courtship dance with handkerchief play and ritual links to arrullos and alabaos.
currulao.insight: Currulao is integral to UNESCO's 'Marimba music, traditional chants and dances from the Colombia South Pacific region and Esmeraldas Province of Ecuador' (file 01099): inscribed via Decision 5.COM 6.8 (Nairobi, 2010) and extended on 2 December 2015 in Windhoek to include Ecuador (UNESCO ICH).

cuban-rumba.name: Cuban Rumba
cuban-rumba.profile: Cuban rumba is a secular Afro-Cuban genre of music, dance and song that originated in urban Havana and Matanzas in the late 19th century, rooted in African (Abakua, Yuka/Congo) and Spanish-derived (coros de clave) traditions. The rumba complex comprises three forms: yambu (slow, couple), guaguanco (couple, featuring the vacunao pelvic thrust), and columbia (fast, solo, male, acrobatic, linked to Abakua). Performed with tumbadoras, lead quinto, claves, palitos/cata and call-and-response vocals (English Wikipedia; UNESCO).
cuban-rumba.insight: 'Rumba in Cuba' was inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List in 2016 (file 01185); UNESCO notes it historically acted as an expression of self-esteem and resistance (UNESCO).

al-ayyala.name: Al-Ayyala
al-ayyala.profile: Two rows of ~20 men with thin bamboo canes (as spears) face each other while drummers between play; men sway heads and sticks and chant poetry, simulating battle. Joint Oman/UAE, UNESCO 2014. Composite performing art (poetry+drum+dance).

al-razfa.name: Al-Razfa
al-razfa.tagline: Antiphonal chants and choreographed rifle movements of the UAE and Oman
al-razfa.profile: Al-Razfa is a traditional performing art practiced across the United Arab Emirates and the Sultanate of Oman. Performed by men of all ages and social classes during weddings and national festivals, the art features two facing lines of performers creating a dual chorus led by a main singer. Dancers move in the space between the rows, executing choreographed movements while holding wooden replica rifles, while young girls sometimes swing their hair to the music. Historically a victory celebration, it now serves as a popular social entertainment transmitted directly within families.
al-razfa.insight: Once a communal celebration of battle victory, Al-Razfa pairs two facing rows of men chanting Nabati poetry with dancers wielding wooden replica rifles.
al-razfa.profile_long:
Al-Razfa is a traditional performing art practiced throughout the United Arab Emirates and the Sultanate of Oman. Originally performed as a communal celebration of victory, the dance has evolved into a popular form of social entertainment performed at social occasions such as weddings and national festivals.

The structural formation of Al-Razfa consists of male performers forming two facing lines, with dancers filling the central space between them. Led by a main singer, the two rows establish a dual chorus that sings chants in an antiphonal, call-and-response manner. Many of these chants consist of verses from traditional Nabati poetry, carefully selected to fit the specific occasion.

During the performance, dancers execute choreographed movements while holding wooden replica rifles in their hands. In some instances, young girls participate by swinging their long hair in time to the music. Musicians accompany the singers and dancers using drums and other instruments, with modern practitioners adapting musical instruments and composing new melodies to appeal to younger audiences.

Al-Razfa is inclusive of all ages and social classes, with performers ranging from heads of State and elders to young children. Knowledge and skills are transmitted directly within the family through observation and active participation during social gatherings, where individual roles are learned through practice.

burundi-royal-drum.name: Ritual Dance of the Royal Drum
burundi-royal-drum.tagline: Sacred drumming-and-dance that once crowned Burundi's kings
burundi-royal-drum.profile: The ritual dance of the royal drum is a Burundian spectacle combining powerful synchronized drumming with dancing, heroic poetry and song (UNESCO; Wikipedia). At least a dozen drums, always an odd number, are arranged in a semicircle around a central Inkiranya drum; surrounding Amashako drums keep a continuous beat and Ibishikiso drums follow, while two or three drummers dance to the rhythm. Drummers enter and exit balancing the heavy drums on their heads. In ancient Burundi drums were sacred objects reserved for rituals such as coronations and royal funerals.
burundi-royal-drum.insight: The ingoma tradition dates to the 17th century and honored the monarchy — a king was said to have "ascended the drum." It was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2014 (9.COM); a 2017 Presidential decree subsequently restricted performance to male players only.
related: Royal drum traditions of the Great Lakes

nijemo-kolo.name: Nijemo Kolo
nijemo-kolo.tagline: Silent circle dance of the Dalmatian hinterland.
nijemo-kolo.profile: A closed-circle couple dance from the Dalmatian hinterland (Dalmatinska zagora) of southern Croatia, performed essentially without musical accompaniment - the rhythm set by the dancers' steps. Male dancers lead female partners in vigorous, spontaneous, seemingly rule-free steps that publicly test the woman's skill; the lead is the kolovoda. It may be framed by ojkanje, rera or ganga singing or the diple (twin-reed shepherd's flute). Danced at fairs, weddings, carnivals and saint's-day celebrations (English Wikipedia; UNESCO).
nijemo-kolo.insight: Inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List in 2011 (file 00359); its silence may have originated as a way for peasants to dance despite prohibitions, the rhythmic thumping of shoes itself a form of defiance (UNESCO).

alardah-alnajdiyah.name: Alardah Alnajdiyah (Saudi Ardah)
alardah-alnajdiyah.profile: Saudi men’s performance combining dance, drumming and chanted poetry; two facing rows of sword-bearing men with drummers and a flag-bearer, a poet chanting antiphonally. Originally a pre-war Najdi tribal dance. UNESCO 2015.

fa-ataupati.name: Fa’ataupati
fa-ataupati.tagline: The rhythmic Samoan slap dance mimicking the swatting of mosquitoes.
fa-ataupati.profile: The Fa’ataupati is a vigorous Samoan men's dance characterized by synchronized body percussion. Performed without external instruments, the dancers use their own bodies as drums through forceful slapping of the chest, thighs, and arms. It is the only all-male dance in Samoa and requires significant physical strength and stability. Traditionally, dancers apply heavy amounts of coconut oil to protect the skin from the intensity of the rhythmic strikes.
fa-ataupati.insight: The dance originated in the 19th century as a rhythmic response to a mosquito invasion, turning the act of slapping insects off the skin into a percussive art form.
fa-ataupati.profile_long:
The Fa’ataupati stands as a unique percussive tradition within the Samoan archipelago, distinguished by its lack of external musical accompaniment. Developed in the 19th century, the dance is a physical manifestation of everyday survival; it is said to have been born from the arrival of mosquito swarms in the Kingdom. The word 'pati' translates to 'clap,' while 'Fa’ataupati' refers to the act of forcefully clapping or slapping. What began as the practical, frantic movement of swatting biting insects was eventually codified into a disciplined, synchronized performance of strength and coordination. 

In performance, the Fa’ataupati is an exhibition of male vitality. Dancers perform in groups, as the dance is rarely seen as a solo endeavor. The music is generated entirely by the performers' bodies: the sharp crack of palms against the chest, the duller thud of slaps on the thighs, and the rhythmic stomping of feet against the ground. Because the slapping is forceful enough to leave physical marks, performers traditionally coat their bodies in coconut oil to provide a protective layer and a characteristic sheen. 

While rooted in 19th-century history, the Fa’ataupati remains a vital part of Samoan cultural identity and has influenced modern performance art. It has transitioned from village squares to international stages, notably being integrated into the repertoire of contemporary dance companies like Black Grace in New Zealand. Despite these modern adaptations, the core of the dance remains unchanged—a high-energy, percussive display that requires the dancers to move in perfect unison, maintaining a steady tempo through physical impact alone.

taualuga.name: Taualuga
taualuga.tagline: The apex of Samoan performance art and the ceremonial finale of the Fa'amatai system.
taualuga.profile: The Taualuga is the most prestigious dance in Samoa, serving as the grand finale for weddings, social functions, and cultural festivities. Traditionally performed solo by the daughter (taupou) or son (manaia) of a high chief, it represents the pinnacle of refinement and aristocratic poise. The performance is defined by graceful hand gestures and a stately demeanor, often contrasted by the boisterous, spontaneous antics of 'aiuli' dancers who perform alongside the soloist.
taualuga.insight: The name refers to the topmost rafter of a traditional house; just as that beam completes a home, this dance completes a ceremony.
taualuga.profile_long:
The Taualuga stands as the centerpiece of Samoan culture, a dance that signifies the successful conclusion of a monumental task. Its name is derived from the final stage of building a traditional fale (house), specifically the securing of the topmost rafter. In the social hierarchy of the Fa'amatai system, the dance was historically the domain of the village's most high-born youth. The taupou, the daughter of a high chief, was raised from childhood to master this art, which served as a public testament to her virtue, her family’s status, and her training in chiefly protocol. While the manaia (the chief's son) could also perform, his version was often more lighthearted and lacked the strict requirements of elegance demanded of the taupou.

A performance of the Taualuga is a sensory display of Samoan wealth and history. The dancer is traditionally clad in an 'ie toga, a finely woven mat decorated with red feathers, and a tuiga—a complex, multi-part headdress that can include nautilus shells, human hair, and turtle shell. The dancer’s skin is anointed with scented coconut oil, creating a cosmetic sheen that catches the light. Before the graceful movements of the Taualuga begin, the dancer may perform an 'ailao,' a display of dexterity involving the twirling of a nifo'oti (hooked blade), which recalls the taupou’s ancestral role leading war parties and ceremonial processions.

Technically, the dance is characterized by its subtlety. Unlike the more energetic group dances that might precede it, the Taualuga focuses on the hands and facial expressions. The soloist maintains a calm, regal posture while the fingers and wrists execute precise, fluid motions. This elegance is intentionally framed by the 'aiuli'—peers or elders who dance in the background with exaggerated, humorous, and loud gestures to highlight the soloist's refinement. During the performance, it is customary for observers to engage in 'lafo,' the practice of throwing or placing money on the dancer as a sign of respect for their skill and lineage, a modern evolution of the traditional gifting of fine mats and tapa cloth.
taualuga.sacred_note: Traditionally reserved for the high-born virgins of the village; it is the pinnacle of ceremonial protocol. Outsiders should treat the performance with high respect and observe the 'lafo' (money gifting) custom if appropriate.

kailao.name: Kailao
kailao.tagline: The fierce Tongan war dance of discipline and mock combat
kailao.profile: The Kailao is a Tongan war dance performed by men wielding stylized wooden clubs known as pate kailao. Originating from the island of ‘Uvea, the dance emulates fighting through fierce, disciplined movements coordinated by a lead dancer's vocal commands. It is distinct for its lack of singing, relying instead on the rhythmic striking of a slit drum or metal tin to set a combat-ready tempo.
kailao.insight: Unlike most Tongan dances, the Kailao is performed in total silence except for a percussive beat, as speaking was historically viewed as a sign of weakness in battle.
kailao.profile_long:
The Kailao stands as a powerful expression of Tongan martial discipline, though its roots lie in the neighboring islands of Wallis and Futuna. Introduced to Tonga in the 19th century, it was quickly annexed into the local culture as a ceremonial display of strength and obedience. The dance is characterized by its aggressive, high-energy movements where men carry the pate kailao—a stylized club that serves as both a rhythmic instrument and a symbolic weapon. Unlike the lyrical and melodic traditions of other Tongan dances, the Kailao is traditionally performed without singing, a reflection of ancient warrior codes where silence was equated with true strength.

In a typical performance, the dancers do not follow a fixed musical score but rather the cues of a lead dancer. This leader calls out specific sequences by name, signaling the group to shift formations, engage in mock combat, or perform intricate tricks with their clubs. The accompaniment is purely percussive, often provided by a beaten slit drum or, in more contemporary settings, a resonant tin box. This stark, rhythmic backdrop emphasizes the precision of the dancers' footwork and the synchronized striking of their weapons.

A modern evolution of the Kailao is the Sipi Tau, the challenge performed by Tongan national rugby teams. While the traditional Kailao is silent, the Sipi Tau incorporates fierce chanting, a change influenced by 19th-century introductions of vocalized war dances. The Sipi Tau was formally penned in its modern form by King Tāufaʻāhau Tupou IV in 1994 to honor the national rugby team. Today, whether performed as a silent ceremonial display or a vocalized sporting challenge, the Kailao remains a vital symbol of Tongan identity and the enduring legacy of South Pacific warrior traditions.

kete-akan.name: Kete
kete-akan.era: Asante royal court tradition (17th-18th century roots)
kete-akan.profile: Kete is a dance-music form originating among the Asante and performed by the Akan of Ghana, originally confined to the palace of the Asantehene and subchiefs entitled to a palanquin (Cambridge University Press; Ejisu Besease). The term refers simultaneously to a set of instruments, the music, and the dance. Danced barefoot by trained dancers with the lapa cloth lowered beneath the chest, its slow, dignified movements use symbolic hand gestures reflecting moral values; the music is reputed to attract good spirits (Cambridge). Individual pieces include Adaban, Apente and others, performed at royal funerals, festivals and durbars.
kete-akan.insight: Per R.S. Rattray's early-20th-century notes, Kete was 'taken to war' and played at Adae ceremonies, funerals and formerly at executions; the full Kete ensemble was the prerogative of the Asantehene (academic analysis of Asante Kete drumming).

intore.name: Intore
intore.profile: Rwanda’s iconic warrior dance ("the chosen ones"), historically performed by elite trained men of the Tutsi military for the Mwami; dancers wear sisal-fibre manes and ankle bells and carry spears, performing vigorous leaps. Royal/martial origin = ethnographic record.

umushagiriro.name: Umushagiriro
umushagiriro.profile: Rwandan women’s "cow dance" honouring cattle heritage through slow graceful arm and body movements imitating the long-horned Inyambo cattle; dancers wear flowing umushanana and perform to drum and song.

xibelani.name: Xibelani
xibelani.tagline: An indigenous Tsonga women's dance of rapid hip-shaking and voluminous skirts.
xibelani.profile: The Xibelani dance is an indigenous tradition performed primarily by Tsonga women from the Mpumalanga and Limpopo provinces of South Africa. Dancers tie a voluminous skirt, known as a tinguvu, around their waist to emphasize rapid, rhythmic hip movements. Historically rooted in the coastal traditions of southern Mozambique, the dance is accompanied by traditional percussion, hand clapping, whistles, and modern Tsonga disco.
xibelani.insight: Tracing its roots to 15th-century southern Mozambique, the dance's name translates from Xitsonga as "hitting to the rhythm."

xibelani.profile_long: The Xibelani dance, also known regionally by variants such as Shibelani, Shibelana, or Shibelane, stands as an indigenous cultural expression of the Tsonga women. Originating from the Mpumalanga and Limpopo provinces of South Africa, the name itself is derived from the native Xitsonga language, roughly translating to "hitting to the rhythm" as encapsulated in the concept "xi Bela ni vunanga." While the term "xibelani" primarily describes the specific dance style, it is frequently used interchangeably to refer to the distinctive skirt worn during the performance. The history of this artistic form stretches back into the early coastal eras of southern Mozambique, dating from the 1400s or earlier, when local tribes experimented with wooden percussion instruments, drums, xylophones, and marimbas. The indigenous Chopi people became particularly renowned in this tradition through their development of the timbila, an instrument and musical form officially registered in the UNESCO heritage archives as a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity. In performance, dancers engage the entire body to guide their movements while locking their hip shakes precisely to the percussion rhythm. Historically, musicians playing the mbila xylophone and swigubu drum formed an ensemble alongside call-and-response vocalists, while women took turns dancing directly in front of the orchestra. The traditional skirts of earlier eras were constructed from various fibers, wool, strings, and grass. In contrast, modern tinguvu are constructed from strong cloth and wool, often woven by hand or machine, designed with vibrant colors and patterns that create a dramatic swirl when the hips move. The methodology shares affinities with a fast-paced Caribbean shake combined with intricate Tsonga choreography. Traditionally, Tsonga girls learn xibelani as a vital expression of cultural pride. It is performed during specific cultural occasions such as mkhinyavezo and Ku chachula, alongside other traditional forms like makhwaya and mchongolo. While women traditionally dance xibelani while men perform makhwaya or xincayinciy, modern societal shifts see men participating as well, particularly during festive gatherings known as xiseveseve. Today, the dance is embraced openly across diverse settings, appearing in church services, community rituals, and modern musical spaces featuring Tsonga disco and Tsonga ndzhumbha.

cheraw.name: Cheraw (Bamboo dance)
cheraw.tagline: Mizoram's clapping-bamboo dance of rhythm and balance
cheraw.profile: Cheraw is the traditional bamboo dance of the Mizo people of Mizoram, considered one of the oldest Mizo dances with origins possibly dating to the 1st century AD (Wikipedia). Six to eight people, usually men, hold pairs of long bamboo staves laid across horizontal bamboos on the ground and clap them rhythmically while female dancers step intricately in and out, avoiding the closing poles; movements imitate swaying trees and flying birds. Women wear the vakiria headdress, thihna necklace, kawrchei blouse and puanchei sarong. Once a ritual for the soul of a mother who died in childbirth, it is now performed at festivals such as Chapchar Kut (Wikipedia; Amar Chitra Katha).
cheraw.insight: On 12 March 2010 Mizoram set a Guinness World Record for the largest bamboo dance when 10,736 people performed Cheraw in unison - 2,518 at the Assam Rifles Ground and 8,218 along the streets of Aizawl (Guinness World Records).

dhamal-sufi.name: Dhamal
dhamal-sufi.tagline: A rhythmic Sylheti folk circle dance celebrating the union of Radha and Krishna.
dhamal-sufi.profile: Dhamal is a traditional folk dance and music form originating from the Sylhet and Mymensingh regions of Bangladesh. Primarily performed by women during weddings and auspicious events, it features a circular formation and rhythmic clapping. The dance is deeply rooted in the devotional themes of Radha and Krishna, symbolizing the spiritual union of the soul.
dhamal-sufi.insight: During the dance, participants are removed in a process resembling musical chairs as the tempo accelerates, mirroring the intense, escalating devotion of the Radha-Krishna narrative.
dhamal-sufi.profile_long: Dhamal, also known as Dhamail, is a folk music and dance tradition prevalent in the Mymensingh and Sylhet regions of northeastern Bengal, in present-day Bangladesh. The tradition is deeply historical, with references to the term appearing in the works of 14th-century poet Chandidas, 16th-century poet Dawlat Wazir Bahram Khan, and 17th-century poet Daulat Qazi. The introduction of the dance to the Sylhet region is credited to folk music composers Radharaman Dutta and Arkum Shah. The dance is primarily performed by women during marriages and other auspicious occasions. The structure of the performance involves a circular formation where participants move while clapping their hands to the beat of the music. The musical accompaniment, typically provided by men, includes instruments such as the mirdanga and kartals. The vocal structure follows a leader-chorus format, where a leader sings the lyrics first, followed by the others. The thematic content of the songs centers on the love of Radha and Krishna, with the inner significance of the dance representing the union of souls for a newly wedded couple. A distinctive feature of the dance is its escalating tempo and dynamics, which build to a peak. During this process, the dance incorporates a mechanic similar to musical chairs, where dancers are removed one by one as the speed increases. Breaks are integrated into the performance to allow the participants to consume paan, areca nut, or tea.

casino-cuban.name: Casino
casino-cuban.tagline: Cuban-style salsa, basis of Rueda de Casino.
casino-cuban.profile: Casino (known since the 1970s as Cuban salsa / salsa cubana) is a partner dance developed in Havana in the early-to-mid 1950s, named after the casinos deportivos dance halls. A circular (rather than slotted) partner dance, it fuses Son Cubano footwork with figures from Cuban mambo, cha-cha-cha, rumba guaguanco and North American jive, traditionally danced contratiempo. Dancers improvise references to Afro-Cuban folklore (Orisha gestures, rumba). It is the basis of Rueda de Casino, a round dance with a caller and frequent partner changes (English Wikipedia).
casino-cuban.insight: Casino's spontaneous integration of Afro-Cuban dance vocabulary (rumba, Orisha gestures) within a partner dance distinguishes it sharply from the slotted, linear North American salsa styles (English Wikipedia).

mapale.name: Mapale
mapale.profile: A fast, energetic Afro-Colombian dance of the Caribbean coast (Magdalena River banks, Cartagena, San Basilio de Palenque), named after the Cathorops mapale fish whose out-of-water movements inspired the steps (Wikipedia; Sounds and Colours). Driven by tambor alegre and tambora with handclaps and singing; emphasizes rapid hip and torso isolation and athletic improvisation. Originally a fishermen's night dance, later more sensual in character.
mapale.insight: Declared Patrimonio Cultural Inmaterial de la Nacion via Ley 2520 of 2025, together with bullerengue and son de negro (Infobae; Congreso de Colombia).

bullerengue.name: Bullerengue
bullerengue.profile: An Afro-Colombian baile cantado (sung dance) of the Caribbean coast (Bolivar, Cordoba, Sucre, Antioquia; San Basilio de Palenque area), led by elder women cantadoras in a call-and-response circle answered by chorus and handclaps (World Music Central; Universidad de Antioquia). Entirely percussive: tambor alegre (hembra), tambor llamador (macho), maracas; women dance in wide polleron skirts. Born in palenques (Maroon communities) as a vehicle of memory and resistance.
bullerengue.insight: George List made the oldest known field recording of bullerengue in Evitar, Bolivar, in 1964; the dance was declared Patrimonio Cultural Inmaterial de la Nacion by Ley 2520 of 4 August 2025, alongside mapale and son de negro (El Tiempo; Congreso de Colombia).

carimbo.name: Carimbo
carimbo.tagline: Afro-Indigenous circle dance and drum music of Para, Amazon.
carimbo.profile: Carimbo is a dance, drum and music genre originating in the 17th century in northern Brazil, centered on Para around Marajo Island and Belem. Named after the curimbo drum (Tupi for 'hollow stick that produces sound'), it blends African syncopation, Indigenous Amazonian circle dancing/maracas and Portuguese elements. The dance is loose and flirtatious: women in long rounded skirts spin while a man tries to retrieve a dropped handkerchief with his mouth. Registered as Intangible Cultural Heritage of Brazil by IPHAN on 9 November 2014 (English Wikipedia; IPHAN).
carimbo.insight: IPHAN registered carimbo as national heritage on 9 November 2014; the 'King of Carimbo' Pinduca is among its most popular performers (English Wikipedia).

dai-peacock-dance.name: Peacock Dance of the Dai
dai-peacock-dance.tagline: Graceful Dai dance mirroring the sacred peacock
dai-peacock-dance.profile: The Peacock Dance (孔雀舞, Kongque wu) is the most famous folk dance of the Dai people of Yunnan, imitating the movements of the peacock, a Dai totem of auspiciousness and beauty (English Wikipedia; CITS). Traditional forms include a heavy bamboo-and-silk peacock-frame dance and an 'unarmed' version, accompanied by elephant-foot drums, gongs and cymbals. It features flexible knees and expressive arm, wrist and finger work, performed at festivals such as Water-Splashing.
dai-peacock-dance.insight: Listed in 2006 in China's first batch of national intangible cultural heritage, it embodies Dai spiritual values and was made world-famous by dancer Yang Liping (China Odyssey Tours; English Wikipedia).

horon.name: Horon
horon.profile: Group folk dances of Turkey’s Eastern Black Sea region in circle/line formation with rapid footwork, jumps and shoulder shimmies; from Greek choros, Pontic Greek roots, 50+ regional variants, typically to kemençe or tulum. NOT UNESCO — the 2021 inscription claim is false.

halling.name: Halling
halling.profile: Vigorous Norwegian men’s folk dance (bygdedans) of Hallingdal and Valdres; fast and acrobatic, often solo (laus), with leaps, spins and feats of strength. Signature move is the hallingkast — kicking a hat held high on a stick. Grieg composed halling pieces. NOT UNESCO.

zonaradiko.name: Zonaradiko
zonaradiko.tagline: A Thracian belt-hold line dance that twists into tight spirals and fast steps
zonaradiko.profile: Zonaradiko is a traditional folk dance originating from Thrace in northeastern Greece. Dancers form an open line or circle, gripping the belts of those adjacent to them. The dance is shared across the border in southeastern Bulgaria, where it is known as Pravo or Pravo Trakijsko Horo. Following the 1923 Treaty of Lausanne, Zonaradiko served as a primary cultural touchstone for diverse Greek populations settling in the Evros region.
zonaradiko.insight: Named after the zonari or belt that dancers hold, this open-circle dance anchored displaced communities across Evros following the 1923 Treaty of Lausanne.

video_stack.title: Greek Dance of Thrace Region "Zonaradikos" by National Dance Ensemble "Romiosini"
Zonaradiko Greek Dance
Dance tutorial ''Zonaradikos'' from Greece

zonaradiko.profile_long:
Zonaradiko is an open-circle folk dance native to the historical region of Thrace in northeastern Greece. Its defining feature is its grip: rather than linking hands or shoulder-to-shoulder holds, dancers reach across to grip the zonaria—the cloth belts or sashes—worn around the waists of the participants on either side. Executed with bent knees throughout, the dance moves in a 12-count pattern comprising 8 basic steps, shifting between slow steady progression and rapid accelerations.

In regional practice, particularly across the northern Evros prefecture, Zonaradiko holds a prominent place in social gatherings. Following the population exchanges mandated by the Treaty of Lausanne in 1923, the Evros area received wave after wave of incoming groups, including indigenous Thracians, refugees from Bulgarian and Turkish Thrace, Pontic Greeks, and Cappadocians. In this multi-ethnic mosaic, Zonaradiko acted as a unifying medium of shared identification across diverse migrant backgrounds.

Across Thrace, local variations dictate the structural evolution of the line. In western Thrace, men historically lead the front of the line while women follow toward the rear. As the sequence nears its climax, the lead dancer spirals the line inward into the center, winding the circle tightly around himself before unwinding the chain back into an open circle. In northern Thrace, the steady tempo of the primary Zonaradiko frequently accelerates into a fast-paced transition known as the tsestos.

During the tsestos phase, structural divisions often occur within the performance space. Dancers either transition together into rapid tsestos footwork, or a secondary belt-hold line forms inside the original circle toward the center. Historically, men would step out to perform the intense tsestos steps in an inner ring while women either paused to watch or maintained the steady Pravo rhythm in the outer circle.

malambo.name: Malambo
malambo.tagline: Competitive solo gaucho footwork duel of the Pampas.
malambo.profile: Malambo is a solo, traditionally all-male competitive gaucho dance from the Pampas, with no formal choreography. Dancers face off in counterpoint, displaying elaborate percussive footwork - zapateados (stomping) and cepillados (brushing) - often with spinning boleadoras and accompanied by guitar and bombo (English Wikipedia). Two main styles exist: estilo sureño (southern) and estilo norteño (northern, faster). The first musical version was published by Ventura Lynch in 1883.
malambo.insight: Malambo is the central solo expression of gaucho identity; the National Malambo Festival has been held in Laborde, Córdoba, since 1966, and the troupe Malevo brought it to a global audience on America's Got Talent in 2016 (English Wikipedia).

matachines.name: Matachines
matachines.tagline: A ritual sword-dance of European origin adapted by Native and Mestizo communities.
matachines.profile: The Matachines are a tradition of ritual dancers found from Peru up to northern New Mexico, blending European sword-dance roots with Indigenous practices. Emerging in Spain during the sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries from traditions like the moresca, the dance was introduced to the Americas by Spanish missionaries as an evangelizing tool. Performers wear ceremonial attire and masks to enact narratives featuring characters such as El Monarca, La Malinche, and El Toro. Today, the societies dance to venerate saints, Mother Mary, or the Holy Trinity while celebrating native peoples' faith and culture.
matachines.insight: In Bernalillo, New Mexico, Matachines dancers have performed for over three hundred years to enact the ancient battle between good and evil.

video_stack.title: Matachines ABQ Rosa de Guadalupe
Matachines
The Matachines dance to honor La Virgen de Guadaulpe
matachines matamoros en reynosa.wmv

matachines.profile_long:
The Matachines dance emerged in Europe during the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, closely related to the moresca and the bouffons described by Thoinot Arbeau in his 1589 Orchésographie. In 1642, Juan de Esquivel Navarro documented the tradition in his treatise Discursos sobre el arte del dançado. A sword dance resembling a matachin was even performed at Hampton Court on January 6, 1604, by Scottish courtiers before James VI and I and the French ambassador. Transported to the Americas by Spanish missionaries, the dance served as an evangelizing tool, introduced as the Dance of the Moors and Christians. In Bernalillo, New Mexico, the Matachines de San Lorenzo have maintained continuous performances for more than three hundred years.

The dance features a distinct cast of characters dressed in ceremonial attire. El Monarca typically represents Moctezuma or another tribal leader, supported by two to four captains acting as main generals. La Malinche appears as the Native or Mestizo woman, while El Toro symbolizes the malevolent comic man or Satan, draped in buffalo skins and wearing the horns of a sacred ancestor. Alongside Abuelo and Abuela—the grandfather and grandmother—and a chorus of dancers, the performance portrays Moctezuma's desertion of his people, his luring back by La Malinche's smiles, the eventual reunion, and the final slaying of El Toro, who is blamed for all mischief.

While oral history among Pueblo tribes connects the dance to the Moors and Christians, its significance transformed outside the Iberian peninsula. Participants dance for profound religious purposes, venerating Mother Mary—such as Our Lady of Guadalupe—local saints, Christ, or the Holy Trinity, represented by a three-forked Sword of the Holy Trinity. All cultural artifacts associated with the performance are explicitly blessed by a priest. The fundamental narrative opposes good and evil, with good ultimately prevailing, serving as a celebration of native peoples and their salvation through faith and culture.

Performers wear traditional ceremonial clothing, with masks that vary significantly from village to village and tribe to tribe. In central Mexico, the tradition is also known as matlachines and matlatzines. From the Yaqui communities to the Pueblos of New Mexico and southward into Peru, the dance has adapted to local cultures while maintaining recognizable formations. Though dance steps differ among distinct peoples, the spatial formations remain broadly similar, reflecting a shared historical root forged in colonial encounters.

saltarello.name: Saltarello
saltarello.profile: Lively Italian dance in fast triple metre named for its leaping step; first recorded in the late-14th/early-15th-c. Tuscan manuscript British Library Add MS 29987. Survives as a couples’ folk dance played on zampogna or organetto with tamburello. Distinct from the pizzica/tarantella family. NOT UNESCO.

padayani.name: Padayani
padayani.tagline: Kerala Bhadrakali temple ritual of painted kolams
padayani.profile: Padayani (Padeni) is a ritual folk art of Bhadrakali (Bhagavati) temples of Central Travancore, Kerala, commemorating the dance performed to pacify goddess Kali's rage after she slew the demon Darika (Kerala Tourism). Its hallmark is the kolam - large masks/effigies painted on arecanut palm spathes in natural pigments (green, carbon-black, turmeric-yellow, vermilion) representing figures such as Bhairavi, Kalan (death), Yakshi and Pakshi. Evolving from the healing ritual Kolam Thullal, it involves the Kaniyar (Ganaka) community for lyrics and costume and Nair performers, with percussion on the patayani thappu, chenda and para. It is performed from roughly mid-December to mid-May at temples like Kadammanitta (G. Venu, Natana Kairali).
padayani.insight: Padayani is distinct from Theyyam: it is centred on Bhadrakali temple festivals of southern/central Kerala and on impermanent areca-spathe kolams, whereas Theyyam belongs to North Malabar and embodies deities directly (Kerala Tourism).

hula-kahiko.profile: Hula composed before Western influence, accompanied by oli (chant) and percussion (ipu heke, pahu). Suppressed after American Protestant missionaries arrived 1820; revived under King Kalakaua’s 1883 coronation. Sacred/religious hula = ethnographic record only.

hula-kahiko.sacred_note: Sacred hula requires ritual seclusion during learning and absolute precision in performance; errors are seen as spiritually dangerous. Lei used in sacred dance are often left as offerings on an altar to Laka.

hula-auana.name: Hula ʻauana
hula-auana.tagline: The modern evolution of Hawaiian storytelling through song and stringed instruments.
hula-auana.profile: Hula ʻauana is the modern evolution of Hawaiian dance, emerging in the 19th and 20th centuries through the integration of Western musical influences. Unlike the austere, percussion-driven kahiko style, ʻauana is characterized by melodic singing (mele) and the use of stringed instruments like the guitar and ukulele. The dance serves as a visual dramatization of song lyrics, using fluid hand gestures to represent natural elements and human emotions.
hula-auana.insight: Meaning 'to wander' or 'drift', this style replaced sacred drums with the melodic harmony of guitars and ukuleles to tell stories of the post-1800s world.

hula-auana.profile_long:
Hula ʻauana represents a significant cultural shift in the Hawaiian Islands, marking the transition from ancient ritual protocols to a modern performance art influenced by Western contact. The term 'ʻauana' literally translates to 'to wander' or 'drift,' reflecting how the dance moved away from the rigid, sacred requirements of the heiau (temples) and the strict protection of the goddess Laka. This evolution was driven by the introduction of Christian morality and Western melodic harmony, which transformed the vocal delivery from rhythmic chanting (oli) into strophic, melodic songs. 

In a typical performance, the dancers act as visual storytellers. While the feet maintain a steady rhythmic base through steps like the kāholo and hela, the hands and arms perform the primary narrative work. A dancer's hands might mimic the swaying of a tree in the breeze, the cresting of an ocean wave, or internal states such as yearning and fondness. This style is often performed in a 'luna' (standing) position, though 'noho' (sitting) variations exist. The subject matter of ʻauana is vast, ranging from praise for significant people and places to the expression of contemporary emotions, moving beyond the genealogical and mythological focus of ancient forms.

Musical accompaniment is the defining feature of the genre. The heavy, sharkskin-covered pahu drums of the past are replaced by a portable acoustic string section. The ukulele provides the rhythmic heart, while the steel guitar—a uniquely Hawaiian innovation involving a steel bar to mute and slide across strings—accents the vocalist with its characteristic sliding tones. A double bass typically maintains the underlying pulse. Despite these modern tools, the core philosophy remains rooted in the 'mele' (poetry); the dance exists to serve the words, ensuring that the oral traditions of Hawaii continue to adapt and survive in a changing world.

hula-auana.sacred_note: While ʻauana is generally less ritually restricted than kahiko, it is still deeply rooted in Hawaiian spirituality and the concept of mana in language. Dancers should respect the mele (poetry) and the cultural protocols of the hālau.

kapa-haka.name: Kapa haka
kapa-haka.tagline: Māori performing arts suite uniting choral song, haka, and synchronized poi dance.
kapa-haka.profile: Kapa haka is a dynamic Māori performing-arts suite combining choral singing, action songs, haka challenges, and traditional poi dances. Tracing its roots to pre-European forms and 1860s tourist concert groups, modern practitioners compete biennially at the national Te Matatini festival. Mixed groups synchronize posture, footwork, and hand gestures to assert community heritage and identity.
kapa-haka.insight: Performers wield tennis-ball sized poi on cords—modern ones fashioned from plastic shopping bags—while singing in European-style harmony.
kapa-haka.profile_long:
Kapa haka translates literally to group ('kapa') and dance ('haka'), representing an essential avenue for Māori people to express and showcase their cultural Polynesian identity. Modern kapa haka traces back to pre-European times, evolving out of traditional forms such as haka, mau rākau weaponry, poi ball swinging, and mōteatea chants. The contemporary presentation format emerged in the 1860s, particularly in Rotorua concert groups catering to tourists, blending traditional Māori principles with European musical concepts.

A full kapa haka performance can last up to 40 minutes and consists of a coherent suite of songs and dances. These items include waiata tira warm-up songs, whakaeke entrance songs, waiata-ā-ringa action songs, haka challenges, mōteatea old-style singing, poi coordinated swinging dances, tītī tōrea stick games, and whakawātea closing songs. Each item type may appear multiple times across a single performance, executed by mixed groups of several to dozens of individuals connected by family, iwi, or school associations.

The music is primarily vocal, structured around European-style harmony with guitar accompaniment, alongside traditional vocal declamations and body percussion like foot stamping. Instruments are limited to the guitar, pūtatara conch shell, and the percussive sounds of poi striking hands and rākau sticks hitting the floor. Performers maintain strict synchronisation, with distinct roles such as male and female kaitataki leaders guiding the group, alongside specialized composers, choreographers, and costume designers.

Key movement styles include the haka, performed in triple metre with aggressive facial expressions like the pūkana glaring, and the waiata-ā-ringa, which feature the wiri hand trembling to signify the interface between mind and body. Women's poi dances showcase grace and coordination, utilizing cords up to a meter long where performers manipulate multiple balls simultaneously. Traditional mōteatea unison songs preserve historical, genealogical, and cultural information through laments and lullabies.

Every two years, adult performers from across New Zealand gather for Te Matatini, the country's premier national kapa haka competition. Youth groups similarly compete at events such as the national secondary schools competition, maintaining a high standard of performance across generations.

nauru-frigate-bird-dance.name: Frigate Bird Dance (Nauru)
nauru-frigate-bird-dance.profile: Among documented Nauruan dances (with dogoropa and the historical fish dance, the latter surviving only in photographs); circular reigen dances noted; much eroded by colonial influence. Recorded by David Fanshawe ("Frigate Bird Dance, Nauru," Spirit of Polynesia 1993).

baamaaya.name: Baamaaya
baamaaya.era: Origins in an early-19th-century drought (per oral tradition)
baamaaya.tagline: Dagbamba social dance with men in feminine attire
baamaaya.profile: Baamaaya, meaning 'the river/valley is wet', is the most popular social dance-drumming of the Dagbamba (Dagomba) of Dagbon in Northern Ghana (Ghana Goods; Wikipedia: Dagbon music and dance). Oral tradition links its origin to a severe drought when men dressed in women's clothing to appease the land gods for rain; the costume is notable for male cross-dressing. It is danced mainly by men wearing the cowrie-beaded 'yebsa' waist belt and metallic anklets, with named sections (e.g., Baamaaya Sochendi, Sikolo, Kondoliya). Instruments include the gungon bass drum, lunga talking drums, container rattles and the wia notched flute (Ghana Goods).
baamaaya.insight: Ethnomusicologist David Locke's late teacher Alhaji Abubakari Lunna doubted the popular cross-dressing origin story, suggesting the frenetic motions instead derive from waving off mosquitoes (Tufts University, Dagomba Dance Drumming).

kazukuta.name: Kazukuta
kazukuta.tagline: Luanda's masked carnival dance with cane and umbrella
kazukuta.profile: Kazukuta is a traditional dance of Luanda, central to the city's Carnival, performed in groups (often in circles) to drums, marimbas and occasional brass. Its characteristic step is a slow tap-dance: the dancer shifts weight between heel and toe while leaning on a cane or umbrella (Mundo da Dança; Paraná State arts portal). Dancers wear striped trousers and ornamented military-style jackets and masks caricaturing animals to lampoon the oppressor, and the rhythm is kept on cans, dikanzas, bottles and barrel hoops.
kazukuta.insight: Together with semba, rebita and kabetula, kazukuta is one of the Luanda dance-music styles that fed into modern Angolan music; historically it served as a form of veiled protest, letting Angolans mock colonial authority through masquerade (FM Afro; Música de Angola).

kiba-dinaka.name: Kiba / Dinaka
kiba-dinaka.profile: Peak of Pedi/Northern Sotho musical expression; men each blow an end-blown aluminium pipe (naka) of a different pitch to produce a harmonized descending melody with energetic dance; women’s version (kosša ya dikhuru) involves kneeling and torso movement. Survived apartheid as a migrant genre. Dual music+dance.

mendiani.name: Mendiani
mendiani.era: Traditional; featured in Les Ballets Africains from the 1950s
mendiani.tagline: Malinke initiation dance for a chosen young girl dancer
mendiani.profile: Mendiani (Mandiani, Manjani) is a social dance of the Malinke (Maninka) people of Upper Guinea - especially the Siguiri region - and Mali (ethnomusicology citing Eric Charry; Mande Drum and Dance). Traditionally a chosen pre-pubescent girl, regarded as the village's best dancer, is initiated into the Mendiani society; she relinquishes the title at puberty and chooses a successor. Carried on young men's shoulders to the rhythm Denadon while wearing a large boubou and mask, she removes them as the drummers switch to Mendiani and performs highly acrobatic, graceful steps to djembe and dunun (Mande Drum and Dance; pancocojams).
mendiani.insight: Ethnomusicologist Eric Charry notes Mendiani is 'associated with young girl dancers in upper Guinea (the region of Siguiri especially)', usually cited as the tradition's source, just as Kouroussa is cited for Dundunba (Cuyahoga CC / Charry).

bikutsi.name: Bikutsi
bikutsi.tagline: Beti 'beat-the-earth' dance of stamping rhythm and candor
bikutsi.profile: Bikutsi is a musical and dance genre of the Beti (Ewondo) people around Yaoundé, Cameroon; the name means roughly "beat the earth" (bi- plural, -kut- to beat, -si earth), describing a dance of foot-stamping (Wikipedia; ChinAfrica). It is built on an intense 6/8 rhythm and was historically performed by women who gathered to sing candidly about their lives — relationships, sorrows and social commentary — clapping and stamping in unison, later adapted to balafon and electric guitar.
bikutsi.insight: Bikutsi originated as a women's form of self-expression in a male-dominated society and was revolutionized for international audiences in 1987 by Les Têtes Brûlées, whose guitarist Zanzibar muted his strings to mimic the balafon; it now rivals makossa as Cameroon's most renowned style (Wikipedia; ChinAfrica).

zinli.name: Zinli
zinli.tagline: Fon funeral drum-dance of the Abomey plateau
zinli.profile: Zinli (formerly Avi-Zinli) is a Fon funeral rhythm and dance from the Abomey plateau of Benin, created in the 19th century by Prince Gbinyin — the future King Glèlè (reigned 1858–1889) — for the funeral of a friend of his father, King Guézo (Numeridanse; CID). It is danced with lightness and flexibility to the zin (a vase-shaped drum that gives the rhythm its name), supported by gongs, rattles, hand-claps and song; an academic study notes a distinctive 24/8 metric structure with instruments including the kpezinga, kpezinvi and gan bells.
zinli.insight: Long reserved for funerary use, zinli was popularized from the 1980s by the artist Alèkpéhanhou (Michel Loukou), "the king of renewed Zinli," carrying a sacred Dahomean court tradition to wide popular and international audiences while remaining an intangible cultural marker of Abomey identity (Numeridanse; academic study).

ingoma-mapiko.name: Ingoma ya Mapiko
ingoma-mapiko.profile: Masked celebratory dance of the Makonde, central to puberty-to-adulthood initiation; masked male dancers, drums and provocative call-and-response choir. UNESCO Urgent Safeguarding 2023 — insurgency in Cabo Delgado halted festivals. Sacred initiation = ethnographic record.

luddi.name: Luddi
luddi.tagline: A celebratory Punjabi folk dance of victory, weddings, and communal joy.
luddi.profile: Luddi is a traditional folk dance originating in the Punjab region, spanning both eastern India and western Pakistan. Danced by men and women of all ages, it marks occasions of victory at weddings and sports events. Participants move in circles, pairs, or groups while clicking their fingers, clapping, jumping, and executing half-turns to the music of the dhol and shehnayi.
luddi.insight: Performed in circles to the sound of the dhol, Luddi celebrates triumph at weddings and sports matches across Punjab.
