french-cancan.name: French Cancan
french-cancan.tagline: High-kicking Parisian music-hall dance of the Moulin Rouge.
french-cancan.profile: The can-can (cancan) is a high-energy music-hall dance that emerged in working-class Parisian dance halls; per Britannica it was popular in Parisian dance halls in the 1830s and appeared in variety shows and revues from the 1840s, in lively 2/4 time danced at first to quadrille or galop music. It evolved from the final figure of the quadrille and the galop. Signature moves are the high kick (battement), rond de jambe, port d'armes, cartwheel and grand ecart (jump splits), with vigorous skirt-and-petticoat work. Choreographer Pierre Sandrini formalized the staged 'French Cancan' at the Moulin Rouge in the 1920s and his Bal Tabarin from 1928 (Wikipedia; Britannica).
french-cancan.insight: The tune most associated with it is Offenbach's 'Infernal Galop' (1858, from 'Orphee aux Enfers'); per Wikipedia it was never officially banned, despite the legend (Wikipedia).

musette.name: Musette (bal-musette)
musette.era: From the 1880s in Paris; peak to 1945; decline ~1960; revival since
musette.profile: Bal-musette is a style of French popular music and dance that became popular in Paris from the 1880s, centered on the accordion and the working-class dance halls of the Bastille (rue de Lappe) and the guinguettes (Wikipedia). Auvergnat immigrants first danced the bourree to the cabrette bagpipe (locally 'musette') and hurdy-gurdy; Italian immigrant accordionists later transformed the scene, the accordion displacing the bagpipe. Its repertoire of close-embrace 'musette-form' dances includes the valse-musette (with the toupie variation), tango-musette, paso-musette, polka, mazurka and the java. Performers include Antoine Bouscatel, Emile Vacher, Charles Peguri and Gus Viseur; the 1930s saw cross-pollination with Django Reinhardt's gypsy jazz.
musette.insight: More a scene/style than a single dance - by 1945 it was the most popular style of dance in France before declining sharply around 1960 (Wikipedia).

java.name: Java
java.era: Developed early 20th c.; peak in bal-musette c.1910-1960
java.tagline: Fast, close Parisian bal-musette waltz of the early 20th century.
java.profile: The java is a dance developed in France in the early 20th century, probably evolving from the valse (waltz), mainly performed in bal-musette halls between roughly 1910 and 1960 (Wikipedia). It arose from demand for an easier, faster, more sensual waltz that did not require a large hall - couples dance very close, taking small advancing steps in 3/4 time. Its provocative close hold led some 'respectable' bals-musette to ban it. It is played on the musette accordion; the name's origin is uncertain (one folk etymology links it to the Auvergnat pronunciation of 'Ca va?'). A java features in a cafe scene in Jean Vigo's film 'L'Atalante' (1934).
java.insight: The java is the one wholly original dance to emerge from the bal-musette scene rather than an adaptation of an existing ballroom dance (Wikipedia, Bal-musette).

gigue.name: Gigue
gigue.era: 17th c. (imported into France from the British/Irish jig); Baroque suite movement
gigue.tagline: Lively Baroque suite-closing dance; the French form of the jig.
gigue.profile: The gigue (Italian giga) is a lively Baroque dance originating from the British/Irish jig, imported into France in the mid-17th century, where it usually appears as the final movement of the instrumental suite (Wikipedia; Britannica). It is usually in 3/8 or a compound metre (6/8, 6/4, 9/8, 12/8), often in fugal/contrapuntal texture with accents on the third beats. The French gigue was light and ornamented; the Italian giga faster and more virtuosic. The gigue was probably never a court dance but was danced by nobility on social occasions; in early French theatre, performances customarily ended with a gigue. Bach's suites and Pachelbel's 'Canon and Gigue' are well-known examples.
gigue.insight: This is primarily a musical form / stylized concert dance rather than a living folk dance - Britannica notes true jigs were quick and wild solo dances while gigues were danced by couples in formal ballet style (Britannica).

rigodon.name: Rigodon
rigodon.era: 17th-c. folk dance; court dance under Louis XIV; Baroque form 17th-18th c.
rigodon.tagline: Lively duple-time couple dance of Provence/Dauphine; also Baroque form.
rigodon.profile: The rigaudon (rigodon; anglicized rigadoon) is a French dance in lively duple metre, musically similar to the bourree but rhythmically simpler with regular (often eight-bar) phrases (Wikipedia). It originated as a sprightly 17th-century folk couple dance associated with the southern provinces of Vivarais, Languedoc, Dauphine and Provence, and became a court dance under Louis XIV, remaining fashionable in French and English courts through the 18th century before yielding to the minuet. The traditional couple choreography uses brisk hopping/skipping steps (pas de rigaudon), facing partners with raised arms and foot-stamps. In Provence it was played by the galoubet-and-tambourin; in Dauphine it persisted as a fiddle tradition and crossed to Quebec folklore. Campra, Rameau and Ravel ('Le Tombeau de Couperin') used it (Wikipedia; Wikipedia FR).
rigodon.insight: Like the bourree and gavotte, it spans a living southern-French folk tradition and a stylized Baroque suite movement; the Wikidata item explicitly flags itself 'different from' a separate genre/form-term entity (Wikidata).

hivinau.name: Hivinau
hivinau.era: Old but post-contact (name likely from English 'Heave now!')
hivinau.profile: The hivinau is danced in two concentric circles (one of men, one of women) turning around a central orchestra and group leader. A male soloist calls a short verse and the chorus answers in heightened speech ('Hiri, haa, haa'); when dancers meet they turn and perform knee or hip shakes. Themes typically concern fishing and the sea. It often opens or closes a festival or transitions between dances and is considered the least technically demanding ori Tahiti form (English Wikipedia; Society of Folk Dance Historians).
hivinau.insight: Though old, it is 'not traditional' in origin - the name probably derives from the European sailors' cry 'Heave now!' at the anchor capstan (English Wikipedia).

paoa.name: Paoa
paoa.tagline: Seated Tahitian circle dance with a soloist couple.
paoa.profile: The paoa is a dance in which performers kneel or sit in a circle, sing and tap their thighs to a repetitive scanning refrain (patautau), while a selected boy and girl dance inside the circle. It is traditionally linked to tapa (barkcloth) making - women beat bark in rhythm and sang to break the monotony. Themes are usually hunting or fishing; being chosen for the central solo is an honor signifying a teacher's recognition (English Wikipedia; The Tahiti Traveler).
paoa.insight: The seated, thigh-slapping format derives from the communal rhythm of beating bark to make tapa cloth (The Tahiti Traveler).

laendler.name: Landler
laendler.era: Rose to popularity late 18th c.; direct ancestor of the waltz
laendler.tagline: Alpine couple turning dance, ancestor of the waltz.
laendler.profile: The Landler is a European folk dance in 3/4 time. Couples turn under each other's arms with complex hand-holds, dance back to back, and rotate in closed hold to moderate triple-time music (Styrian harmonica, fiddle, zither). It originated in the rural Alps - Wikidata records its country as Switzerland, Germany and Austria - with its name from the 'Landl' district of Upper Austria. It strongly influenced the waltz and appears in works by Mozart, Beethoven and the Strauss family (English Wikipedia; Britannica).
laendler.insight: It is more Austrian/Alpine than specifically German - a shared Austria/Germany/Switzerland dance and the direct rustic predecessor of the Viennese waltz (Britannica; English Wikipedia).

zwiefacher.name: Zwiefacher
zwiefacher.era: Term first documented 1780; older melodies predate the modern bar line
zwiefacher.tagline: Bavarian couple dance with changing meter.
zwiefacher.profile: The Zwiefacher is a southern German couple turning dance with quick tempo and changing meter, alternating between 3/4 (waltz) and 2/4 (Dreher/pivot) - and occasionally polka - beats, in regular or irregular patterns. Couples turn rapidly in a closed (often barrel) hold. It is danced mainly in Lower Bavaria, the Hallertau and the Upper Palatinate, and is also known in the Black Forest, Austria, Alsace, the Czech Republic and Sudetenland. Accompaniment is accordion, fiddle and brass; lyrics served as mnemonics. Researcher Felix Hoerburger catalogued 112 tunes carrying 474 different names (English Wikipedia).
zwiefacher.insight: The name (loosely 'twofold'/'double') may refer to the two alternating meters or to the couple being tightly wound together; the dance was added to Germany's Nationwide Inventory of Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2016 (English Wikipedia).

discofox.name: Discofox
discofox.tagline: Popular German social partner dance to disco/Schlager.
discofox.profile: Discofox is a social partner dance that evolved in Europe in the mid-1970s as a rediscovery of the closed dance hold within the otherwise solo-dominated disco scene, roughly contemporaneous with the American hustle. The beginner's basic step is 'step-step-tap' (advanced dancers split-beat a four-step basic over three beats of music). It is danced to 2/4 or 4/4 music - 1970s disco, Eurodisco, Italo disco, pop, techno and Schlager - and is hugely popular at parties, weddings and dance schools in Germany, Austria and Switzerland (English Wikipedia; Danceflavors).
discofox.insight: Its spread was greatly boosted by the 1977 film 'Saturday Night Fever'; it remains a staple of German Schlager party culture (English Wikipedia).

zeibekiko.name: Zeibekiko
zeibekiko.era: Late 17th-c. origin (Zeybek militia); popularized on the Greek mainland after 1922
zeibekiko.profile: A solo, improvisational Greek folk dance related to the Turkish zeybek dance, named after the Zeybeks (irregular Aegean militia of the Ottoman Empire). First seen in the late 17th c. in Constantinople and Smyrna; originally a dance for two armed men, it became a solitary improvised dance. Rhythmic pattern 9/4 or 9/8. After the 1922 population exchange it spread on the mainland via laiko/rebetiko. Traditionally male and introspective (the 'eagle dance'), danced solo within a circle of seated, clapping companions; now also danced by women. Accompanied by bouzouki and baglamas (English Wikipedia; GTP Headlines).
zeibekiko.insight: The zeibekiko was added to Greece's National Inventory of Intangible Cultural Heritage in March 2022 alongside the bouzouki, tzouras and baglamas; it is danced to rebetiko, the music genre UNESCO inscribed in 2017 (GTP Headlines, 24 Mar 2022).

ikariotikos.name: Ikariotikos
ikariotikos.era: Traditional island dance; popularized nationally via a 1975 song by Giorgos Konitopoulos
ikariotikos.tagline: The fast island chain dance of Ikaria.
ikariotikos.profile: A traditional chain folk dance and accompanying song from the island of Ikaria in the NE Aegean. Danced in an open circle/line, men and women holding hands (older form, crossed palms) or by the shoulders. Structured in parts: slow walking steps (akin to Sta Tria), then steps resembling the Issios of Kalymnos, then fast steps with full leg-and-body mobility; duple 2/4 rhythm. Historically sung, then accompanied by Cretan/island lyra, the Ikarian tsampouna (bagpipe), and violin with laouto/mandolin; today also guitar, bouzouki and accordion. Danced at weddings, baptisms and religious festivals (English Wikipedia; ResearchGate ethnographic study).
ikariotikos.insight: Some specialists hold that the original Ikariotikos was slow and the fast popular version is effectively a Ballos; its modern fame owes much to Giorgos Konitopoulos's song 'My love in Ikaria,' notably performed by Yiannis Parios (English Wikipedia).

hasaposerviko.name: Hasaposerviko
hasaposerviko.tagline: The fast 2/4 'Serbian butcher's dance' form of hasapiko.
hasaposerviko.profile: The fast version of the hasapiko, in 2/4 meter, also called grigoro hasapiko ('fast hasapiko'); the name references Serbian and other Balkan influences. A line/open-circle dance with hands on shoulders, easier and quicker than the slow hasapiko, with changing steps - an expanded, transformed motif of the hasapiko. Accompanied by bouzouki-led ensembles and common in rebetiko/laiko; it forms the fast climactic section of the sirtaki sequence and of many taverna dance sets (English Wikipedia: Hasapiko; Dance Museum).
hasaposerviko.insight: Hasaposerviko is treated within the Hasapiko article on English Wikipedia rather than as a standalone topic; sources describe it as the fast (2/4) hasapiko expanded with Balkan/Eastern-European traits (Leontis, 'Culture and Customs of Greece'; Dance Museum).

gwoka.name: Gwoka
gwoka.era: Originated 17th c. (slavery); rehabilitated post-1946 and from the 1960s-70s; UNESCO 2014
gwoka.tagline: Guadeloupe's emblematic Afro-Creole drum, song and dance tradition.
gwoka.profile: Gwoka is the umbrella Afro-Guadeloupean tradition combining responsorial singing in Guadeloupean Creole, rhythms played on the ka drums, and improvisational dance. It is generally played with three drums - two lower-pitched 'boula' carrying the central ostinato and one higher 'make'/marqueur (soloist) that dialogues with the dancer - accompanied by chacha (gourd rattle) and tibwa (sticks). Built on seven base rhythms, it is performed in the lawonn (circle) at the lewoz night gathering, where dancers enter one at a time to face the drums while the public claps and sings the chorus. It emerged on sugar, coffee and banana plantations and became a symbol of resistance and Guadeloupean identity (UNESCO; Repriz/ZoukJam).
gwoka.insight: Gwoka was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List on 26 November 2014; ethnomusicologist Jerome Camal notes that because Guadeloupe is a French overseas department without a UN seat, the petition had to be sponsored by the French state, and the campaign was led from 2004 by Felix Cotellon of the centre Repriz (Camal, Intl Journal of Heritage Studies, 2016; UNESCO).

lewoz.name: Lewoz
lewoz.tagline: Warrior gwoka rhythm and the night drum gathering.
lewoz.profile: Lewoz is one of the seven base gwoka rhythms - a combative/warrior rhythm in two-time, historically said to have set the rhythm for attacks on plantations and to function as an incantation dance, marked by a strong dialogue between dancer and make. The word also names the traditional night gathering (the lewoz / sware lewoz), held traditionally on Friday or Saturday until dawn, where participants form the lawonn circle around the ka drums, chacha and singers; dancers enter one by one to face the drums while the crowd claps and sings the response (Wikipedia; BNF France Ameriques).
lewoz.insight: Lewoz is considered the reference rhythm and the preferred space of expression of gwoka; the English Wikipedia entity describes the lewoz event/performance tradition (rural musical performances of Martinique and Guadeloupe, as opposed to gwo ka moderne) rather than narrowly the rhythm.

kaladja.name: Kaladja
kaladja.tagline: Slow gwoka rhythm of sorrow, hardship and love.
kaladja.profile: Kaladja is one of the seven gwoka base rhythms, typically slow, expressing suffering, sadness, mourning, reflection and love; it is used at funeral wakes (veillees) and can be danced as a couple dance. Like the rest of the repertoire it is played on the ka drums (two boula plus make) with chacha and responsorial Creole song, danced within the lawonn at lewoz gatherings. Dancers perform slower, mournful gestures echoing the grief and hardship of enslaved communities (Wikipedia: Gwo ka; ZoukJam summarizing Repriz).
kaladja.insight: Kaladja's slow, somber character makes it the gwoka rhythm most associated with laments and funeral wakes, contrasting with the festive toumblak and mennde.

toumblak.name: Toumblak
toumblak.tagline: Joyful gwoka rhythm of love, fertility and celebration.
toumblak.profile: Toumblak is among the best-known of the seven gwoka rhythms, a lively, festive rhythm associated with love, fertility, joy and the earth, generating sensual, undulating hip movements and suggestive postures. A faster, accelerated variant is called toumblak chire. Played on the ka drums (two boula plus make soloist) with chacha and responsorial Creole song, it is danced in the lawonn circle during lewoz gatherings and is often compared to African fertility dances such as the kalenda (Wikipedia: Gwo ka; Comite du Tourisme des Iles de Guadeloupe).
toumblak.insight: Toumblak is frequently described as the most famous and widespread gwoka rhythm, embodying celebration and courtship amid the hardship of enslaved life.

padjanbel.name: Padjanbel
padjanbel.tagline: Gwoka work rhythm tied to sugarcane cutting.
padjanbel.profile: Padjanbel (also padjabel, granjanbel, gwadjanbel) is one of the seven gwoka base rhythms, a work rhythm in 3/4 whose jerky movements recall the gestures of enslaved plantation workers, especially the cutting of sugarcane; it is also described as a women's rhythm symbolizing grace, pride and liberation, linking earth and sky. Played on the ka drums (two boula plus make) with chacha and responsorial Creole song, danced in the lawonn at lewoz gatherings (Mulaogwada; Wikipedia: Gwo ka).
padjanbel.insight: Padjanbel is the gwoka rhythm most explicitly tied to sugarcane-cutting labor, though some traditions reinterpret it as a warrior dance.

graj.name: Graj
graj.tagline: Gwoka work rhythm miming manioc/cassava preparation.
graj.profile: Graj (grage) is one of the seven gwoka base rhythms, a work rhythm linked to agricultural labor whose movements evoke the phases of grating manioc into cassava flour and field harvesting; it is generally slower, with the reprise marked, and is sometimes danced by women as a seductive dance. Played on the ka drums (two boula plus make) with chacha and responsorial Creole song, danced in the lawonn circle during lewoz gatherings (Wikipedia: Gwo ka; Loka Guadeloupe).
graj.insight: Graj's choreography directly imitates the grating of manioc (grage manioc), making it one of the clearest examples of gwoka as embodied memory of plantation labor.

woule.name: Woule
woule.profile: Woule (roule) is one of the seven gwoka base rhythms and the only one in triple time (3/4), a swaying, airy waltz-like 'rolling' rhythm sometimes danced with a scarf (foulard); it is often described as a 'Creole waltz' used to charm and mimic/satirize the European masters, and is also associated with repetitive work like graj. Played on the ka drums (two boula plus make) with chacha and responsorial Creole song, danced in the lawonn at lewoz gatherings (Wikipedia: Gwo ka; Ziloka).
woule.insight: Woule's waltz-like triple meter is widely cited as evidence of European ballroom influence creolized into the gwoka repertoire.

mende.name: Mennde
mende.era: Said to be the last of the seven rhythms to arrive (post-1848 abolition); living tradition
mende.tagline: Fast carnival gwoka rhythm of Congo/African origin.
mende.profile: Mennde (mende, minde) is one of the seven gwoka base rhythms, a fast, energetic carnival rhythm symbolizing collective celebration and escape (evasion); it incites a marching/parading pace and underlies the polyrhythms of Guadeloupean Carnival. It is said to be the last rhythm to arrive on the island, brought by contracted 'Congos' after the 1848 abolition, and shows strong direct African influence. Played on the ka drums (two boula plus make) with chacha and responsorial Creole song, danced in the lawonn during lewoz gatherings and in carnival processions (Wikipedia: Gwo ka; Mediatheque Caraibe/Lameca).
mende.insight: Mennde is the gwoka rhythm most embedded in Carnival; its African/Congo origin story marks it as the most recent addition to the seven-rhythm canon.

biguine.name: Biguine
biguine.profile: Biguine is a rhythmic dance and music style of the French Antilles, originating in Saint-Pierre, Martinique in the 19th century and shared with Guadeloupe. It fuses West African bele drumming with 19th-century French ballroom dance steps; the orchestrated biguine is defined by the interplay of clarinet and trombone, while the drum biguine (bidgin bele) uses the bele drum and tibwa sticks with call-and-response nasal singing. Danced as a close couple dance with a roll of the hips. It reached Paris after the 1931 Colonial Exhibition via stars like Alexandre Stellio and Sam Castandet (Wikipedia; Smithsonian Folkways).
biguine.insight: Biguine is widely cited as one of the ancestors of the jazz developed by Creoles of New Orleans. Cole Porter composed 'Begin the Beguine' in 1935; it gained fame chiefly via Artie Shaw's 1938 swing arrangement, a best-selling record (Wikipedia).

kwadril-gwadloup.name: Quadrille (Guadeloupean)
kwadril-gwadloup.era: Introduced 18th c. (European colonists); creolized 19th c.; revived 1980s
kwadril-gwadloup.tagline: Antillean Creole contredanse-derived figure dance with a caller.
kwadril-gwadloup.profile: The kwadril (Creole quadrille) is a folk figure dance of the French Lesser Antilles derived from the European quadrille/contredanse, performed in Guadeloupe in sets of figures by four couples in a square, directed by a commandeur/konmande (caller) who announces the figures. Guadeloupean sets (balakadri/balkadri) combine proper quadrilles with creolized 19th-century couple dances - biguines, mazouks (mazurkas) and valses creoles. Instrumentation includes accordion, violin, guitar, tanbou dibas, chacha, malakach, triangle, tibwa and the syak (one-metre bamboo rasp). It was creolized by enslaved and freed Africans, who added African rhythms to the European ballroom forms (Wikipedia; CTIG).
kwadril-gwadloup.insight: Antilleans regard the quadrille not as a colonial relic but as a 'new creation' adopted and transformed by people of African descent into a shared symbol of Creole identity across Guadeloupe, Martinique, Dominica and St. Lucia.

dollu-kunitha.name: Dollu Kunitha
dollu-kunitha.era: Traditional; rooted in the Halumatha (Kuruba) Purana
dollu-kunitha.tagline: Karnataka's vigorous Kuruba drum dance for Beereshwara
dollu-kunitha.profile: Dollu Kunitha is a major drum dance of Karnataka performed chiefly by men of the Kuruba Gowda community, centred on the worship of the deity Beereshwara/Beeralingeshwara, a form of Shiva, around Chitradurga and Shivamogga (Wikipedia). Large double-headed drums (dollu), made from neem or palm with goat and sheep hide, are slung from the dancers' waists or necks and beaten with stick and hand while a group of 12-16 dancers move in circular and semi-circular formations led by a singer-conductor, often ending in a human chain (Amar Chitra Katha). Its origin myth, from the Halumatha/Kuruba Purana, tells of the demon Dolla-asura from whose skin Shiva fashioned the first drum.
dollu-kunitha.insight: Embedded in temple worship - in Beereshwara temples the dollu hangs from the ceiling and is beaten at every act of worship - the dance is now performed across communities at festivals such as Maha Shivaratri and Ganesh Chaturthi (Village Square; Wikipedia).

hojagiri.name: Hojagiri
hojagiri.era: Traditional; evolved from the ritual Hodagiri
hojagiri.tagline: Reang women's balancing dance on earthen pitchers
hojagiri.profile: Hojagiri is a folk dance of the Reang (Bru) clan of the Tripuri people of Tripura, performed by a team of four to six women and young girls who sing while balancing on earthen pitchers and managing props - a bottle on the head, an earthen lamp in the hand - moving only the lower half of the body (Wikipedia; Prepp). It is danced during the Hojagiri festival (Mailuma/Laxmi Puja) on the full-moon night after Durga Puja, honouring goddess Mailuma (Lakshmi) for a good harvest. Men sing the lyrics and play the kham drum and sumui flute. Dancers wear the handwoven pachra and rea with coin necklaces and silver ornaments (Historified; The Northeast Today).
hojagiri.insight: Folk artist Satyaram Reang (1943-2023), who dedicated his life to the dance and ran a Hojagiri school, received the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award (1986) and the Padma Shri (2021) for preserving the form (Wikipedia: Satyaram Reang).

baalan-dance.name: Baalan Dance
baalan-dance.tagline: Devotional storytelling and rhythmic dance of Nepal's Brahmin and Chhetri communities.
baalan-dance.profile: Baalan Dance is a traditional devotional dance form from Nepal, practiced primarily by the Brahmin and Chhetri (Kshatriya) communities. It features group singing of bhajans and dramatic reenactments of episodes from Hindu epics, including the Ramayana, Mahabharata, and Krishna Charitra. Accompanied by the rhythmic beats of the khaijadi drum, dancers perform during sacred occasions such as Satyanarayan Puja and Ekadashi, as well as during spontaneous gatherings in rural areas. The art form functions both as a spiritual offering and as a medium for preserving cultural narratives across generations.
baalan-dance.insight: Derived from concepts of divine childhood, Nepal's Baalan dance translates epics like the Ramayana into spontaneous village performances anchored by the khaijadi drum.

baalan-dance.profile_long:
### Origins and History
The term 'Balan' is derived from the Sanskrit 'Balak' and the Nepali 'Bala', referring to childhood. Combined with 'Aayan' (similar to the structure of 'Ramayan'), the term signifies 'Balayan' or stories of divine childhood, serving as a source of joy in later life. Historically developed and maintained by the Brahmin and Chhetri (Kshatriya) communities in Nepal, Baalan acts as a living vessel for epic oral traditions. Dancers reenact sacred lore, passing down religious education and cultural lineage through communal performance.

### How It Is Danced
Baalan is performed collectively in group formations where participants dance and sing in rhythmic synchrony. The movement incorporates theatrical elements, with performers taking on the roles and embodying the implements of various deities and legendary characters. A beginner starts by learning the basic rhythmic steps aligned with the beating of the khaijadi drum while joining the chorus of devotional singing. While it requires structured practice to portray specific epics like the Dasabatar or Krishna Charitra, rural villagers also engage in spontaneous, informal performances during leisure hours.

### Music and Instruments
The music of Baalan relies heavily on vocal bhajans dedicated to Hindu deities such as Vishnu, Ram, and Krishna. The primary instrumental foundation is provided by the khaijadi, a small traditional Nepali frame drum. Dancers and musicians sing in a call-and-response or unified group format, maintaining a steady, structured meter that coordinates the footwork and theatrical gestures.

### Costume and Setting
Performers wear traditional attire suitable for ritual contexts, often carrying specific props or implements that symbolize the deities depicted in the narration. The dance is set in both sacred and informal spaces, ranging from family courtyards during private pujas to village gathering spots during major religious festivals.

### Occasions and Meaning
Baalan is intimately tied to the Hindu religious calendar of Nepal. It is performed during specific observances such as Ekadashi, Chandi Purnima, and Balachaturdashi, as well as during major religious rituals including Satyanarayan Puja, Bhagwat Puran, and Saptaha Puran. Beyond its calendar-based necessity, Baalan serves as a sacred offering (puja), a dramatic retelling of scripture, and a joyful recreational activity for rural agricultural communities.
baalan-dance.sacred_note: Performed as a religious offering during pujas and sacred festivals. Outsiders should observe respectfully during ritual ceremonies such as Satyanarayan Puja and avoid interrupting the devotional singing or sacred proceedings.

sarai-dance.name: Sarai dance
sarai-dance.tagline: A Nepalese weapon dance celebrating divine victory after Dashain tika.
sarai-dance.profile: Sarai dance (also known as Saraya nach) is a traditional Nepalese weapon dance performed predominantly across the western hilly districts of Gulmi, Arghakhanchi, Pyuthan, and Palpa. Executed at religious shrines and temples following Dashain tika, the dance features devotees swinging and clashing traditional weapons like khukuri, swords, and khuda to the accompaniment of Panchebaja instruments. Performers chant 'Wakkhai Wa' while executing rhythmic movements that symbolize the ancient war between gods and demons. The largest gathering takes place on the full moon day at Arje Phulbari in Gulmi.
sarai-dance.insight: Devotees in western Nepal wield real khukuris and swords, clashing metal and chanting Wakkhai Wa at hill shrines after Dashain.
sarai-dance.profile_long:
### Origins and History
Legend holds that the Sarai dance originated to celebrate the victory of divine powers over giants and demons, symbolizing the weapons used in that mythical warfare. Historically, the dance tradition is closely tied to rituals beginning on Saptami, when a colorful flag-adorned image of God, known as an alam, is brought to a temple or kot. This ritualistic display of weapons and divine symbols may have initially served a practical purpose to guard valuable temple statues and armaments. Over generations, the practice evolved into a communal dance performed across the western districts of Nepal, including Gulmi, Arghakhanchi, Palpa, Kapilvastu, Rupandehi, Pyuthan, and Dang.

### How It Is Danced
During the performance, devotees gather at temples and physically swing, display, and clash weapons such as the traditional khukuri knife, swords, and the khuda. The dancers coordinate their movements rhythmically while continuously chanting 'Wakkhai Wa'. Although weapon demonstrations have seen a decline in recent years due to safety concerns, the dance remains intensely vibrant in strongholds such as Dhurkot, Arje, and Isma. The largest performance occurs on the full moon day at Arje Phulbari in Gulmi.

### Music and Instruments
Music for the Sarai dance is provided by Panchebaja, a traditional ensemble of five Nepalese musical instruments. The driving rhythms of the Panchebaja dictate the tempo of the weapon displays, while the collective vocal chants of 'Wakkhai Wa' from the participating devotees resonate throughout the temple grounds.

### Costume and Setting
The setting for the Sarai dance is centered on religious shrines, temples, and kots in the hilly terrain of western Nepal. An integral focal point is the alam, an image of the deity decorated with vibrant colored flags that is placed outside the temple following flower offerings on Saptami. Devotees perform surrounding these sacred spaces while wielding traditional steel weapons offered to the shrine.

### Occasions and Meaning
The dance is intrinsically linked to Dashain, the major Nepalese festival. It typically commences after Dashain tika and is actively performed from the day of Ekadashi through Purnima (the full moon). Beyond its spiritual representation of good triumphing over evil, Sarai dance acts as a historic community gathering that blends sacred puja worship with martial folk tradition.
sarai-dance.sacred_note: Performed at religious shrines during Dashain using consecrated temple weapons; outsiders should respect safety protocols and temple rules regarding weapon handling.

veerabhadra.name: Veerabhadra
veerabhadra.era: Ancient/Medieval origin; documented in modern Goa
veerabhadra.tagline: A fierce ritual dance of divine destruction from the Goa-Karnataka border.
veerabhadra.profile: Veerabhadra is a ritualistic dance-drama performed in Goa, India, primarily during the Shigmo festival and on Chaitra Poornima. The dancer embodies the fierce deity Veerabhadra, born from Shiva's hair to destroy the sacrifice of Daksha. Characterized by Kathakali-style makeup, a massive bamboo halo, and dual swords, the performance migrates from a distant procession into the temple mandap. It represents a historical cultural bridge, blending Kannada traditions with Goan temple rituals.
veerabhadra.insight: At dawn, the dancer collapses in a trance after 'destroying' a theatrical play, only to be revived by temple holy water.

veerabhadra.profile_long:
Veerabhadra is a high-stakes ritual performance that marks the intersection of Goan and Kannada cultural histories. Traditionally performed in regions like Sanguem, Ponda, and Sanquelim, the dance is a living embodiment of the mythological destruction of Daksha’s Yajna. The performer, who inherits the role through specific family lineages, undergoes a rigorous three-day purification process involving fasting and sleeping on the floor before the full moon of Chaitra. This ascetic preparation culminates at midnight when the dancer is transformed through elaborate makeup and costuming, a process that takes place in seclusion to maintain the sanctity of the transformation.

The visual identity of the Veerabhadra is a striking synthesis of regional styles. His face is painted with the fierce, demonic aesthetics of Kerala’s Kathakali, while his head is adorned with a Mysorean-style turban. The most physically demanding element is the prabhavali, a large, decorated halo-like structure made of bamboo and paper tied to the dancer's back, requiring attendants to support its weight during the procession. As the sun begins to rise, the dancer moves toward the temple, accompanied by torchbearers and the rhythmic shouting of 'Horavani' proclamations. The crowd responds with the collective roar of 'Ha Udo', creating an atmosphere of intense religious fervor.

The climax of the ritual occurs at the Vithal Temple in Sanquelim, where the dance interacts with a live theatrical drama. As the Veerabhadra enters the temple enclosure wielding two unsheathed swords, the actors portraying the narrative of Daksha’s sacrifice must flee, signaling the symbolic destruction of the ego and the triumph of Shiva’s wrath. The performance is physically exhausting; the dancer executes specific rhythmic cycles before collapsing into a trance-like state. He is caught by attendants and revived with temple holy water (teerth), a moment that signals the successful completion of the ritual and the conclusion of the festival period.
veerabhadra.sacred_note: The dancer must observe a three-day vow of fasting and isolation. Only specific families may inherit the role.

marchas-populares.name: Marchas Populares
marchas-populares.tagline: The competitive midsummer parades of Lisbon's historic neighborhoods.
marchas-populares.profile: The Marchas Populares are a competitive Portuguese dance tradition originating in Lisbon, where neighborhoods parade through the streets in elaborate, themed performances. Established in their modern form in 1932, these marches celebrate the Midsummer and the feast of Saint Anthony, the city's patron saint. Each district, from Alfama to Alcântara, fields a team of residents who perform choreographed routines to popular music, blending folk motifs with theatrical spectacle. The event is a cornerstone of Portuguese identity, broadcast nationally and serving as the climax of the month-long 'Santos Populares' festivities.
marchas-populares.insight: Every June 12th, Lisbon's rival districts transform the Avenida da Liberdade into a sea of handmade costumes and 'manjerico' plants to compete for the city's most prestigious title.

video_stack.title: Marchas Populares de Santo António 2022
Desfile das Marchas Populares na Avenida da Liberdade

marchas-populares.profile_long:
The Marchas Populares represent the vibrant intersection of neighborhood rivalry, religious devotion, and theatrical performance in Portugal. While historical references to neighborhood marches in Lisbon date back to the 18th century, the modern competitive format was established in 1932 under the direction of José Leitão de Barros. This inaugural event saw three neighborhoods—Campo de Ourique, Bairro Alto, and Alto do Pina—compete on the Avenida da Liberdade, drawing an estimated 300,000 spectators. The success was so immediate that the marches were officialized by the Lisbon City Council in 1934, becoming a permanent fixture of the city's cultural landscape and a frequent subject of Portuguese cinema, such as 'A Canção de Lisboa'.

The structure of the competition is rigorous and spans several months of preparation. Each neighborhood (bairro) develops a unique theme, often incorporating maritime imagery or symbols of Portuguese summer like the 'manjerico' (bush basil) plant. Although the public highlight is the parade down the Avenida da Liberdade on the night of June 12th, the actual judging often takes place days earlier in a closed arena, such as the Altice Arena. Teams are evaluated on specific criteria including choreography, scenography, costumes, lyrics, and musicality. The participants are typically local residents, though they are often led by 'godparents' (padrinhos)—prominent media figures or celebrities associated with the district. 

Musically, the marches are defined by 'popular music' and Fado, often featuring a 'Grande Marcha' (Great March) composed specifically for that year's theme. The atmosphere is one of intense community pride; for one night, the narrow alleys of historic districts like Alfama or Madragoa are emptied as residents take to the grand avenue to defend their neighborhood's honor. The event is inextricably linked with the 'Casamentos de Santo António' (Weddings of Saint Anthony), a mass wedding ceremony held earlier the same day, with the newlywed couples joining the parade. Beyond Lisbon, the tradition has spread to other Portuguese cities like Setúbal, though the Lisbon competition remains the definitive national standard.

the-freddie.name: The Freddie
the-freddie.tagline: A 1960s novelty fad inspired by Freddie and the Dreamers
the-freddie.profile: The Freddie was a short-lived novelty dance that emerged in 1965, sparked by the British Invasion band Freddie and the Dreamers. Characterized by its resemblance to a stationary jumping jack, the dance gained traction in the United States through the band's hit 'Do the Freddie' and a cover by Chubby Checker. Despite its brief peak, the dance became a recognizable cultural shorthand for 1960s fads, appearing in television shows like The Addams Family. Its legacy persists primarily through nostalgic references in film and television rather than active social practice.
the-freddie.insight: A dance so simple it required only the rhythmic extension of legs and arms, it was immortalized by Gomez Addams and later parodied by slasher icon Freddy Krueger.

video_stack.title: The Jackson 5 perform Solos and Medly at the Freddie Prinze show -RARE!

the-freddie.profile_long:
The Freddie represents the peak of the mid-1960s 'fad dance' phenomenon, where a single musical act could trigger a nationwide movement based on a specific set of repetitive gestures. In 1965, the British band Freddie and the Dreamers released 'I'm Telling You Now' and 'Do the Freddie,' the latter reaching number 18 on the United States charts. The dance was inextricably linked to the stage persona of the band's frontman, Freddie Garrity, whose energetic and somewhat eccentric movements provided the template for the dance. The American market, already primed for dance crazes by artists like Chubby Checker, embraced the movement quickly; Checker himself released 'Let's Do the Freddie' that same year, which reached number 40 in the US and number 15 in Canada. 

Technically, the dance is one of the simplest in the novelty canon. It requires no partner and no travel across the floor. The dancer remains stationary, alternating leg extensions with overhead arm movements in a manner that mimics a jumping jack performed without the jump. This simplicity made it ideal for television broadcast, where it was frequently performed on variety shows. One of its most famous early depictions occurred in the 1965 episode of The Addams Family titled 'Lurch, the Teenage Idol,' where Gomez Addams, played by John Astin, performs the dance with characteristic enthusiasm in the family living room.

While the dance's popularity faded as quickly as it arrived, it left a distinct mark on popular culture. It saw a brief resurgence in the 1989 film Troop Beverly Hills, which later led to a lyrical reference in the Rilo Kiley song 'The Frug.' Perhaps the most unusual chapter in its history occurred in 1987, when the slasher film character Freddy Krueger, voiced by Robert Englund, released a song also titled 'Do the Freddy' on the album Freddy's Greatest Hits. This version provided its own set of instructions, pivoting the 1960s innocence of the original into a gimmick for the horror genre. Today, the dance is remembered as a quintessential example of the 'go-go' era, often grouped alongside the Mashed Potato and the Jerk in animated parodies like The Simpsons.

country-swing-dance.name: Country Swing
country-swing-dance.tagline: A high-energy, stationary partner dance defined by aerial lifts and improvisational turns.
country-swing-dance.profile: Country Swing is a partner dance rooted in the Western swing tradition, characterized by its compact footprint and improvisational nature. It utilizes a simplified 'quick, quick, slow' footwork pattern derived from Jitterbug and East Coast Swing. The dance is primarily performed in social settings like bars and clubs, where limited space necessitates a stationary rather than traveling style. Its most distinctive feature is the frequent use of aerial maneuvers, locally referred to as 'lifts'.
country-swing-dance.insight: Unlike the traveling Two-Step, Country Swing is a stationary, rotational dance designed for crowded bars, where simple footwork allows for complex, acrobatic 'lifts'.

Country Swing Dancing **THE BASICS** Tutorial!

COUNTRY SWING DANCING | Basic Steps of Country Swing Dance for Beginners

country-swing-dance.profile_long:
Country Swing emerged as a distinct social partner dance, adapting the expansive movements of traditional swing to the confined environments of country-western bars and honky-tonks. While it shares a musical foundation with Western Swing, the dance itself is defined by its stationary and rotational mechanics. Unlike the Country Two-Step, which travels counterclockwise around the perimeter of a dance floor, Country Swing dancers remain in a fixed spot, making it ideal for crowded venues. The dance's technical foundation is a simplified version of the Jitterbug or East Coast Swing, focusing on a four-step rhythm that allows the lead and follow to maintain balance during rapid rotations.

The hallmark of Country Swing is its reliance on improvisation over fixed patterns. Dancers frequently incorporate 'lifts'—the country-western term for what swing dancers call 'aerials'—where the follower is hoisted into the air. These athletic maneuvers compensate for the simplified footwork and are a central element of the style's visual appeal. Because the dance is often performed in social, non-competitive settings, the connection between partners is fluid, allowing for a wide range of turns and wraps. The dance has seen a resurgence in popularity through social media and viral trends, bridging the gap between traditional country partner dancing and modern urban nightlife.

passinho-do-jamal.name: Passinho do Jamal
passinho-do-jamal.tagline: A viral Brazilian urban dance from Recife blending syncopated footwork and arm gestures.
passinho-do-jamal.profile: Passinho do Jamal is a Brazilian urban dance originating from the Santo Amaro neighborhood in Recife, Pernambuco. Created in 2020 by friends Romero Silva Oliveira Júnior (Jamal) and Pedro Henrique (Eo Chapa), the style draws from brega funk culture and popular street passinhos. Characterized by rapid footwork, a slight hip sway, and synchronized arm movements, it shifted from backyard rehearsals to global social media stardom in the mid-2020s.
passinho-do-jamal.insight: Created in a backyard in Recife as a joke among friends, this syncopated urban dance marched from TikTok straight onto the FIFA World Cup stage.

passinho-do-jamal.profile_long:
Passinho do Jamal emerged in 2020 in the Santo Amaro neighborhood of Recife, Pernambuco, created by childhood friends Romero Silva Oliveira Júnior, known as Jamal, and Pedro Henrique, known as Eo Chapa. Initially rehearsed in a private backyard as a playful pastime, the dance roots itself in brega funk culture and the local "muvucão" dance gatherings. Researcher Thiago Soares notes that brega funk represents a process of jovialization and coreographization geared toward digital platforms. Years after its creation, the dance went viral on TikTok and Instagram, sparking widespread international attention and public debates over digital attribution.

The choreography features a dynamic combination of rapid footwork, changes in direction, and a slight body sway set to syncopated rhythms. The foundational movement sequence relies on stepping to one side, stepping to the other, and taking three steps back, while the arms strictly accompany the movement of the feet. Unlike traditional brega funk styles that emphasize heavy hip isolation, Passinho do Jamal shifts the focus to arm and leg synchrony, creating a playful, marching aesthetic that remains accessible to reproduce visually.

Set to the electronic beats of brega funk, the dance gained prominence through specific tracks such as "Toma Botada" by Eo Chapa and MC Rogê, which climbed the Spotify viral charts, and "Taka La Dentro," which accompanied its arrival as a digital emote in video games like Fortnite. It is danced in diverse contexts, ranging from casual street settings and short-form video platforms to high-profile runways like Rio Fashion Week and global football celebrations.

The dance's cultural footprint expanded massively through digital media, reality television appearances on Big Brother Brasil 26, and international sports arenas during the 2026 FIFA World Cup. Players and national teams across the globe integrated the passinho into their goal and title celebrations, amplifying a cultural movement designed to elevate the visibility of brega funk despite historical local stigmas.

kaze-no-bon.name: Kaze no bon
kaze-no-bon.tagline: A 300-year-old night festival in Yatsuo where unmarried dancers hide their faces from typhoons.
kaze-no-bon.profile: Kaze-no-Bon, meaning "Bon Dance of the Wind," is an annual Japanese festival held from September 1 to 3 in Yatsuo, Toyama, Japan. Tracing its history back more than 300 years to the Genroku era, the festival was originally created to appease typhoons and secure a bountiful rice harvest. At night, young unmarried men and women process through the steep, lantern-lit streets of the village, their faces concealed by flat straw hats. Accompanied by the melancholic tones of the kokyū vièle and the traditional shamisen, the dancers move in long parallel files representing the district's eleven quarters.
kaze-no-bon.insight: In the mountain village of Yatsuo, young unmarried dancers hide their faces beneath low-brimmed straw hats to appease the wrath of the wind gods.

video_stack.title: Owara kaze no Bon Festival Toyama city Yatsuo

kaze-no-bon.profile_long:
Kaze-no-Bon, meaning "Bon Dance of the Wind," is a prominent Japanese festival held annually from September 1 to 3 in Yatsuo, a mountain village located in the extended municipality of Toyama on the western coast of Honshu's main island in Japan. The village of Yatsuo, which had 21,810 inhabitants in 2005, extends around three kilometers along the Ida river, nestled between two mountains. The festival takes place in the steep and cobbled streets of the village center, which are illuminated for the occasion by traditional paper lanterns. Having a history of about 300 years, Kaze-no-Bon has existed without interruption since the Genroku era, spanning from 1688 to 1704. Originally, the festival was held in order to appease Shinto divinities and typhoons, allowing for a bountiful harvest of rice during a period when hurricanes and storms are frequent across the Japanese archipelago.

The festival is uniquely held at night, creating an atmosphere that is sometimes described as eerie or mysterious by onlookers, drawing up to 200,000 visitors from across the archipelago. Long rows of young men and women progress slowly in parallel files, dancing simultaneously to a melancholic melody. Each dancing troupe represents one of the eleven districts of the Yatsuo municipal district. Among the performances, the most traditional dance style is the Kyu odori. Another style is the Shin odori, which was introduced later in 1920; in this newer style, the steps of the men and women differ distinctly, with the men's movements evoking the labor of agricultural field work.

The visual presentation of the dancers is defined by precise costuming. The female dancers are dressed in matching cotton kimonos known as yukata and wear flat straw hats called amigasa, which are heavily tilted to conceal their faces. Their male companions wear a short jacket along with a similar straw hat. These hats and matching kimonos cover the dancers' faces to hide them from the wrath of the god they hope to appease, stemming from the fear that the divine anger might otherwise fall upon them. Traditionally, all participating dancers are unmarried, a custom rooted in old ideas that performers might anger the gods and that the performance acts as a form of virginal self-sacrifice. However, modern interpretations also suggest social reasons, such as providing an opportunity for young unmarried people to meet.

At the rear of the night procession, an older female singer leads the traditional village song known as Ecchu Owara Bushi. This vocal line is accompanied by rare and traditional instruments, including the kokyū, a traditional stringed vièle, a traditional shamisen luth with three strings, and drums. This melancholic music is exceptionally unique to the region and was selected in 1996 by the Ministry of the Environment as one of the 100 soundscapes of Japan. In addition to the main street processions, dance groups perform structured demonstrations on stages scattered throughout the village, while private performances are given in local restaurants and private homes. In the middle of the night, once the tourists have departed, the local population of the town joins the dancers in costume, continuing the celebration sometimes until the break of dawn. Beyond the dance itself, the tiny shops lining the village streets offer games, trinkets, traditional foods, and special Japanese paper as popular souvenirs.

urban-kiz.name: Urban Kiz
urban-kiz.tagline: A Paris-born partner dance shaping Kizomba roots with hip-hop isolations and linear lines.
urban-kiz.profile: Urban Kiz is a partner dance created in Paris during the 2010s that diverged from Angolan Kizomba. Pioneered by dancers such as Curtis Seldon, Cherazad Benyoucef, Enah Lebon, and Moun, it took shape against electronic Ghetto-Zouk, Tarraxinha, and hip-hop remixes. Rather than using the grounded body weight and circular patterns of traditional Kizomba, Urban Kiz emphasizes upright frames, straight legs, sharp directional changes at perpendicular angles, and synchronized isolations. After years of circulating online under names like Kizomba 2.0 and French Style, the title 'UrbanKiz' was adopted in 2015 to establish its own identity.
urban-kiz.insight: Emerging in 2010s Paris, Urban Kiz detached from Kizomba's grounded hips by straightening the legs, tracking geometric lines, and pausing weight transfers through a delayed 'and-principle.'

video_stack.title: ENAH & POCAHONTAS FEAT METHODZ | DOUBLE TROUBLE PART 1 - URBAN KIZ FAM
AZZEDINE & ALLISON - FrenchKiss By Jay Lima (Li Régué #2) URBANKIZ
Audi & Laura - Urbankiz Demo at KZL 2023
What is Urban Kiz? - The Kizomba Channel

urban-kiz.profile_long:
During the 2000s, the Angolan diaspora introduced Kizomba across European hubs, establishing footholds in Portugal, France, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, and Spain. In Paris, social media platforms like YouTube and Vimeo accelerated the cross-pollination of this partner dance with other urban genres. By 2008, the dancer Moun was exploring new dynamics on the floor, followed by Curtis Seldon in 2011 and Enah Lebon in 2012. Around 2013, Seldon and Cherazad Benyoucef systematically altered their posture, connection, and dynamics, crystallizing a distinct way of moving.

For several years, this emerging movement lacked a unified definition. Instructors promoted it under transient labels including Kizomba 2.0, French Style Kizomba, New Style Kizomba, and kizomba fusion. The form deliberately departed from Kizomba’s core technique by absorbing elements of hip-hop and Argentine tango, including pivots and pirouettes. Continued friction over its presentation as authentic Kizomba prompted a decisive break; following disputes in 2015, the name UrbanKiz was formally coined and announced to distinguish the style, where 'Urban' reflects Ghetto-Zouk, R&B, and hip-hop musical textures and 'Kiz' acknowledges its ancestral inspiration.

Technically, Urban Kiz replaces the grounded, continuous weight shifting of traditional Kizomba with high body tension, straight legs, and energetic control. Dancers travel across straight tracks, pivoting sharply at perpendicular angles or reversing directions along linear lanes. Movement stops, foot taps, and isolations synchronize tightly with rhythmic hits, drops, and accelerations. A foundational mechanic is the '&-principle', where advancing or retreating feet do not instantly absorb the body's mass; instead, a preliminary tap places merely 10 to 20 percent of the dancer's weight onto the floor before a controlled, gradual transfer takes place.

The dance's sonic foundation centers on dynamic electronic arrangements including Ghetto-Zouk, Tarraxa, Afrobeat, and contemporary remixes featuring rap and dance music. Rather than following an even, cyclical pulse, Urban Kiz musical tracks incorporate sudden breaks, accelerations, and bridge sections that drop down into slow tempos, challenging partners to execute syncopated contratempos. By 2020, Urban Kiz had expanded from Parisian clubs into an international festival circuit spanning Europe and five other continents.

nae-nae.name: Nae Nae
nae-nae.tagline: A viral 2013 hip-hop dance inspired by a 1990s sitcom character.
nae-nae.profile: The Nae Nae is a hip-hop dance move invented in 2013 by the Atlanta group We Are Toonz with their song "Drop That NaeNae". The movement is defined by placing one arm in the air and swaying from side to side. It draws direct inspiration from Sheneneh Jenkins, an exaggerated character played by Martin Lawrence on the 1990s sitcom Martin. Throughout 2014, the dance achieved massive viral popularity on social media platforms like Vine and YouTube, eventually crossing into mainstream culture via Silentó's 2015 single "Watch Me (Whip/Nae Nae)".
nae-nae.insight: Rooted in a 1990s sitcom character, the Nae Nae exploded across Vine and YouTube in 2013 before becoming a staple of viral sports celebrations.

nae-nae.profile_long: The Nae Nae emerged from Atlanta hip-hop culture in 2013 when the group We Are Toonz released their hit song "Drop That NaeNae". The dance move was explicitly inspired by a character from the 1990s television sitcom Martin, specifically the sassy "ghetto girl" persona Sheneneh Jenkins portrayed by comedian Martin Lawrence in cross-dress. Group member Callamar noted in interviews that the dance encapsulated a funny club-goer persona. Throughout 2014, the dance swept across digital spaces, saturating platforms like Vine, Twitter, Instagram, and YouTube. Its physical execution involves a distinct posture: placing one arm high in the air while swaying the body from side to side. By 2015, the Nae Nae gained an even wider international footprint when American rapper Silentó featured it heavily in his debut single, "Watch Me (Whip/Nae Nae)". Beyond viral internet videos, the Nae Nae permeated professional sports, performed as a celebratory move by athletes at collegiate and professional events. Prominent figures including NBA players, musicians, and politicians like Hillary Clinton and Barack Obama were captured performing or praising the dance. The cultural penetration of the Nae Nae was further solidified when it was integrated as a playable dance move into the video game NBA 2K16.

dongnae-yaryu.name: Dongnae yaryu
dongnae-yaryu.tagline: Traditional Korean masked drama play featuring satire and outdoor performance.
dongnae-yaryu.profile: Dongnae yaryu is a traditional masked drama play in Korea performed for over 120 years in Oncheon-dong, Dongnae-gu. It has been named by the government of Korea as one of the Important Intangible Cultural Properties of Korea. The performance features satire and criticism toward commoners and noblemen, traditionally staged outdoors in a field.
dongnae-yaryu.insight: Performed on the 15th of the Lunar New Year, this masked drama features masks made from gourds and leather covered in mulberry paper.
dongnae-yaryu.profile_long: Dongnae yaryu is a traditional masked drama play in Korea, rooted in the Gyeongsangnam-do province where outdoor theatrical traditions known as yaryu developed. The performance has a history spanning over 120 years in Oncheon-dong, Dongnae-gu, and was historically maintained by a professional theatre troupe called Ohgwangdae. Although its performance tradition was suspended in 1937, it was successfully reorganized in 1950 and subsequently recognized as one of the Important Intangible Cultural Properties of Korea. The event traditionally takes place on the night of the 15th day of the New Year according to the lunar calendar, originally serving as a prayer for farming prosperity and peace, though today it is performed more for celebration and entertainment. The festivities begin with a music group collecting donations from wealthy households at the start of the new year. On the festival day, townspeople gather at bridges such as Busan Bridge and Buma Bridge for a vibrant costume parade leading to the performance site. The parade is led by the character 'Nongjang', followed by other characters and musical bands. Upon arrival at the site, participants color their faces with Chinese ink or don elaborate masks made from gourds or leather, covered with handmade traditional mulberry paper and painted in vivid colors. The core contents of the drama center on biting satire and social criticism directed at both commoners and noblemen. While the specific choreography and dance steps are not documented in available texts, the performance relies on communal participation, masking, and theatrical parade traditions. The tradition connects deeply to the broader heritage of Korean talchum masked dances, preserving local cultural expressions through community organization and festive rituals.
dongnae-yaryu.sacred_note: Originally performed as a prayer for farming prosperity and peace, though in the present day it is performed more for fun.

postmodern-dance.name: postmodern dance
postmodern-dance.tagline: A 20th-century movement that redefined dance as any movement by any person.
postmodern-dance.profile: Emerging in the 1960s, postmodern dance rejected the formal constraints of modern dance in favor of everyday movement and unconventional composition. Centered around the Judson Dance Theater in New York, the movement championed the idea that any person could be a dancer and any movement could be art. By utilizing chance procedures and minimalist aesthetics, choreographers sought to demystify the performance process and challenge audience expectations.
postmodern-dance.insight: Postmodern dance stripped away the proscenium stage and virtuosic technique, asserting that walking, sitting, or standing could be as valid a performance as the most complex balletic leap.
postmodern-dance.profile_long: Postmodern dance emerged in the early 1960s as a radical departure from the compositional and presentational constraints of modern dance. Rather than relying on the emotional expression or technical virtuosity that defined its predecessors, the movement sought to deflate what it perceived as overly pretentious modernist views of art. At its core, postmodern dance asserted that all movement is dance expression and that any person, regardless of formal training, could be a dancer. This philosophy was famously cultivated by the Judson Dance Theater, a collective active in New York City that became the epicenter of the movement. Early postmodern choreographers often employed 'pedestrian movement'—everyday actions like walking, sitting, or standing—to demystify the art form and draw attention away from technique-driven performance. The choreographic process frequently utilized chance procedures, such as rolling dice or tossing coins, to determine the sequence of movements, the number of performers, or their placement on stage. This approach often resulted in dancers hearing the music for the first time during the premiere performance, as the dance and music were treated as independent entities operating by their own logic. By the 1970s, the movement evolved into an 'analytical' phase, characterized by minimalism, conceptual abstraction, and a distancing from expressive elements like costumes and lighting. This period also saw an increased engagement with political activism, including the anti-Vietnam War movement and the feminist movement. By the 1980s, the movement began to reintegrate narrative and historical traditions, though it maintained its influence on contemporary dance and choreographic processes. The legacy of postmodern dance persists in the way it challenged the definition of performance, shifting the focus from the choreographer's ego to an objective, present-time experience.

sprinkler-dance.name: Sprinkler dance
sprinkler-dance.tagline: A novelty dance move mimicking a garden irrigation sprinkler.
sprinkler-dance.profile: The Sprinkler dance is a novelty movement where a dancer places one hand on the back of their neck while waving the other arm and spinning to simulate an irrigation sprinkler. Originating in Australia during the 1980s, the dance gained renewed global fame when the England cricket team adopted it as a bonding exercise during the 2010–11 Ashes series. It subsequently exploded across the internet, featuring in films, television shows, and competitive breakdancing.
sprinkler-dance.insight: In 2024, breakdancer Rachael Gunn brought the garden sprinkler to the Paris Olympics, decades after its 1980s Australian origins.
sprinkler-dance.profile_long: The Sprinkler dance operates as a kinetic imitation of mechanical garden machinery, requiring performers to mechanically cycle their upper bodies while rotating. Accounts of the dance's origins vary, with press coverage in December 2010 tracing its birth to Australia during the 1980s, alongside references to the disco era. The movement involves standing with legs slightly apart and knees slightly bent, bending the left elbow to place the left hand behind the head, and extending the right arm horizontally with a flat, vertical hand. The dancer rotates around the waist in a 180-degree sweep, pulling back three times before swinging the arm back across. Music and specific auditory accompaniments are not detailed in the sources, relying instead on the visual comedy and rhythm of the performer's body. The dance lacks traditional elaborate costumes, typically performed in casual athletic gear, team uniforms, or standard everyday clothing as seen in office spaces and schoolyards. Its primary cultural meaning shifted from a casual 1980s novelty to a potent symbol of team cohesion and viral internet culture. The movement found a home across popular culture, appearing in films such as House Party (1990) and A Night at the Roxbury (1998), television programs like Bluey (2018), and international sports arenas. Notable figures associated with its revival include cricketers Paul Collingwood and Graeme Swann of the England cricket team, as well as breakdancer Rachael Gunn during her 2024 Paris Olympics performance. Regional variants and strict lineages remain minimal, as the dance spread primarily through digital video diaries and social media broadcasting. Gaps in the historical record include any formal musical scores, indigenous roots, or standardized teaching syllabi.

engolo.name: Engolo
engolo.tagline: An ancient Angolan martial art and zebra dance featuring inverted kicks.
engolo.profile: Engolo is a traditional Bantu martial art and combat game originating along the Cunene River in southern Angola. Often called the Zebra dance, practitioners combine high vertical jumps, inverted handstands, and sweeping kicks within a singing, hand-clapping circle. While colonial chroniclers and modern scholars link its techniques to the roots of Afro-Brazilian capoeira, the art remains a distinct expression of Angolan resilience. Documented extensively by artists and researchers in the 20th century, the practice requires both physical agility and a calm spirit.
engolo.insight: In a remote Angolan river basin, fighters emulate the kicking fury of zebras from a handstand, trading blows until one concedes or a ritual specialist halts the match.

engolo.profile_long:
Along the sun-baked banks of the Cunene River in southern Angola, practitioners of engolo gather to test their agility in a dust-ringed circle. In 1950, the Angolan artist Albano Neves e Sousa travelled to Mucope and captured young men executing astonishing inverted kicks and cartwheels in his field sketches. The physical style draws direct inspiration from the natural world, most notably the defensive mechanics and kicking habits of zebras. Engolo functions simultaneously as a martial training method, a celebratory combat game, and a spiritual expression tied to ancestral worldviews.

The historical roots of engolo stretch deep into precolonial Angola, where hand-to-hand combat and evasion tactics were essential for survival. In the late sixteenth century, Jesuit missionaries observed Ndongo warriors leaping with extreme agility to dodge flying arrows and spears. By the mid-seventeenth century, Italian missionary Giovanni Antonio Cavazzi documented regional leaders walking upside down with their hands on the ground and feet in the air to project spiritual authority. Combat training took place inside fortified war camps known as kilombos, forging close-quarters combat skills that later crossed the Atlantic via the slave trade to influence traditions such as capoeira in Brazil, danmyé in Martinique, and knocking and kicking in North America.

Performances of engolo are anchored in an acoustic environment created entirely by participants. Performers stand in a tight circle, providing a steady rhythmic backbone through synchronized hand-clapping, humming, and call-and-response singing. Traditional songs carry sharp aphorisms, such as the declaration that whoever dies in engolo will not be wept for, or a verse praising the vital necessity of agile evasion when no door is available. Occasionally, musicians accompany the circle by playing a musical bow struck against the mouth. The musical meter drives the physical pacing of the match, dictating when a challenger leaps into the center with a sharp shout.

The visual setting of an engolo match is defined by the human circle, known as a roda, which confines the combatants and focuses community energy. Historically, the practice was integrated into major social milestones, including the Efundala, a puberty festival where young women transitioned into adulthood and a victorious fighter earned the right to choose his bride without paying a dowry. Sometimes, a spiritual specialist known as a kimbanda oversees the ring, ensuring that the confrontation remains bound by cultural rules. Competitors enter the space with explosive high jumps—historically honed by vaulting over cattle fences—before dropping to their palms to execute sweeping foot strikes and scorpion kicks.

Technically, engolo relies heavily on inverted positioning, utilizing the ground as an extension of the body's defensive shield. Fighters employ casual terms like mussana and ngatussana for their kicks, and koyola for dragging maneuvers, avoiding any rigid or formalized martial catalog. The foundational movement begins with a powerful baseline jump that launches the body into the air before descending into a handstand or rolling evasion. A practitioner must maintain what elders describe as a light heart; losing one's temper leads to sloppy execution and defeat. Field research by scholars like T.J. Desch-Obi in the 1990s and documentary teams in the 2010s revealed how elderly masters preserved these core sweeping techniques despite decades of disruption caused by the Angolan Civil War.

courante.name: Courante
courante.tagline: A triple-meter Renaissance running dance transformed into a majestic Baroque suite movement.
courante.profile: The courante is a family of triple-meter dances originating in the late Renaissance and flourishing through the Baroque era. Evolving from a fast, jumping Renaissance folk and elite dance into two distinct styles—the majestic, rhythmically complex French courante and the faster Italian corrente—it became a staple movement in the Baroque dance suite, typically placed between the allemande and the sarabande. Characterized by shifting metric accents and an upbeat entry, it captured both courtly solemnity and intimate longing.
courante.insight: Despite its name meaning running, the Baroque French courante was described by Mattheson as the embodiment of sweet expectation and the most serious rhythm.

courante.profile_long:
The courante—also known in various historical spellings as corrente, coranto, or corant—began its life as a lively couple dance in the late Renaissance. In 1589, the French canon Thoinot Arbeau described it as a dance executed with fast running and jumping steps performed by the social elite. Originally functioning as a popular couple dance featuring a pantomime of courtship, it required dancers to move forward, sideways, or occasionally backward with leaping movements that distinguished it sharply from the solemn pavane or basse-dance.

As the aesthetic shifted into the Baroque period, the courante bifurcated into two distinct national styles: the French and the Italian. The French courante, usually notated in 3/2 or 6/4 time, was executed at the slowest tempo of all French court dances. It was marked by profound gravitas, majestic carriage, and intricate metrical ambiguities, particularly hemiolas that blurred the listener's sense of the bar line. Theorist Johann Mattheson characterized the mood of the French courante in 1739 as one of 'sweet expectation,' conveying a heartfelt longing and gratifying hope, while Johann Gottfried Walther noted its rhythm as 'absolutely the most serious one can find.' 

In contrast, the Italian corrente was a significantly faster, more direct, and livelier affair, frequently notated in 3/4 or 3/8 time with a lighter texture. Within the structure of the Baroque dance suite—cemented by masters like Johann Sebastian Bach, Arcangelo Corelli, and George Frideric Handel—the courante invariably followed the allemande as the second or third movement. Whether realized as a stately French meditation in binary form with repeats or a brisk Italian corrente, the dance relied on an upbeat (levée) and alternating simple and double steps that challenged dancers to master sophisticated temporal shifts before the form faded from general use in the late 18th century.

canary-dance.name: Canary dance
canary-dance.tagline: A fiery Renaissance wooing dance of rapid stamps, jumps, and savage theatricality.
canary-dance.profile: The Canary dance was a vibrant Renaissance and Baroque dance that swept European courts after originating from an indigenous Canary Islands template. Characterized by rapid heel-and-toe stamps, energetic jumps, and a thematic framing as a 'savage' wooing game, it appeared in manuals by Caroso, Negri, and Arbeau. By the 17th century, it evolved into a brilliant, technically demanding French theatrical form before fading from popularity.
canary-dance.insight: Dancers stamped so violently it earned the moniker 'frogs legs,' channeling an imagined indigenous Canary Islands fierceness across European courts.

video_stack.title: Understanding Form: The Canary

canary-dance.profile_long:
Rooted in the indigenous traditions of the Canary Islands, possibly related to the Tajaraste, the dance crossed to mainland Spain via enslaved people by 1552, where Diego Pisador noted it at funeral feasts. By the late 16th and early 17th centuries, it captivated French, Italian, English, and Spanish courts, appearing in plays by William Shakespeare and dance manuals by Thoinot Arbeau in 1589, Fabritio Caroso in 1600, and Cesare Negri in 1602. In the 17th century, the French court transformed it into a brilliant, technically demanding specialty before it disappeared from general practice.

Choreographed primarily for a single couple, early versions featured rapid heel-and-toe stamps, deep jumps, and violent movements that earned it the nickname 'frogs legs.' Unlike the rigid court steps of the galliarde, dancers engaged in free improvisation meant to mimic a playful 'savage' indigenous courtship. By the 17th century in France, it incorporated elaborate cabrioles, turns, and battus executed in a fast ternary meter.

Early descriptions like Arbeau's noted simple meters, while Baroque interpretations embraced fast 3/4, 6/8, and dotted rhythms akin to a rapid gigue. Girolamo Kapsberger wrote a famous 1640 virtuoso piece for chitarrone over a three-note basso ostinato, and Gaspar Sanz published a popular version for the Spanish baroque guitar in 1674. Composers such as J.S. Bach integrated its distinctive rhythm into the French Suite in C Minor and the Goldberg Variations.

Performed in Renaissance ballrooms, courtly masques, and theatrical stage productions, dancers wore contemporary court attire while enacting exoticized native themes. The staging frequently highlighted the energetic, unconventional nature of the choreography against structured court environments. Initially functioning as a lively ballroom diversion or theatrical interlude within masques, the dance was framed around the dramaturgical theme of the 'sauvage' or indigenous wooing. Spanish sources like Covarrubias noted its lineage from saltarello-style island dances, while contemporaries relished its bizarre, high-energy spectacle.

Notable figures include dance masters Thoinot Arbeau, Fabritio Caroso, Cesare Negri, Livio Lupi da Caravaggio, and Juan de Esquivel Navarro, who documented its steps. Baroque composers including Girolamo Kapsberger, Gaspar Sanz, J.S. Bach, Henry Purcell, and Jean-Baptiste Lully cemented its rhythmic profile across Europe. It manifested through distinct local variants: Spanish guitar adaptations by Gaspar Sanz, Italian theatrical balletto sequences by Negri and Caroso, and refined French baroque variations emphasizing brilliant footwork and rapid tempos.

lipsi.name: Lipsi
lipsi.tagline: An East German state-invented partner dance designed to immunize youth against rock and roll.
lipsi.profile: Created in 1959 in East Germany, the Lipsi was a state-sponsored social dance designed as a wholesome, socialist alternative to Western rock and roll. Conceived by dance teachers Christa and Helmut Seifert in Leipzig, the dance combined classical ballroom holds with steps borrowed from traditional folk dances like the Ländler and Spinnradl. Despite being patented worldwide and heavily promoted by the government, the dance was poorly received by youth who preferred American music and styles. Protests erupted in cities like Leipzig and Halle, leading to police crackdowns and prison sentences for young dissenters before the dance quietly faded away.
lipsi.insight: Created in 1959 by East Germany to immunize youth against Elvis, the Lipsi became a symbol of state control that young protesters mocked in the streets.

video_stack.title: Gaby Decker tanzt im Lipsi Schritt 1998

lipsi.profile_long:
In the late 1950s, the government of the German Democratic Republic sought to counter the growing popularity of Western youth culture, specifically American rock and roll, boogie-woogie, and Elvis Presley-style gyrations. Publications like 'Der Tanz in der Laienkunst' demanded the creation of new socialist dances that would strip away what authorities deemed bourgeois degeneration and return to traditional folk forms. In 1959, dance instructors Christa and Helmut Seifert introduced the Lipsi at a dance music conference in Lauchhammer. Named after 'Lipsia', the Latin version of Leipzig, the dance was intended to serve as a cultural immunization against capitalist influences.

The dance was written in a 6/4 meter and performed within a classic ballroom dance hold, integrating chassé steps with half-turns, waltz steps, and folk-derived elements. Instructors taught a basic pattern involving side steps and foot taps, accompanied by songs recorded by artists such as Helga Brauer and orchestras led by Kurt Henkels. Rather than fostering enthusiasm, the state's heavy-handed promotion alienated young people who found the rhythm uninspired and the partner mechanics overly rigid. By November 1959, public discontent boiled over when dozens of youths marched through Leipzig chanting slogans in support of Bill Haley and rejecting the Lipsi, resulting in swift arrests and prison terms ranging from months to years.

While regime figures like Hans Bentzien later recalled the Lipsi with amusement as a failed propaganda exercise, its disappearance marked a vivid chapter in the cultural Cold War. Composer Kurt Henkels eventually fled to West Germany to escape state interference, and the Amiga label recordings of Lipsi singles remained historical artifacts of ideological choreography. Decades later, pop artists like Bürger Lars Dietrich playfully referenced the Lipsi in music videos, recalling an era when a simple 6/4 step was deployed as a weapon of state ideology.

cordax.name: cordax
cordax.tagline: Provocative, licentious, and masked comedy dance of ancient Greece.
cordax.profile: The cordax was a provocative, licentious, and often obscene mask dance of ancient Greek comedy associated with drunkenness, revelry, and theatrical performance. Mentioned by writers like Aristophanes, Petronius, and Juvenal, it featured bacchic energy, castanets, and dramatic body movements such as sinking to the ground with tremulous buttocks. It was also linked to the worship of Artemis in Elis, where the goddess held the cult title Kordax. Though condemned as infamous through subsequent centuries, its bouncing trochaic rhythm and unrestrained character left traces across classical and medieval literature.
cordax.insight: Ancient Greek actors performed the cordax wearing masks and oversized, erect artificial penises to entertain audiences during comic plays.
